structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The partial document is the front matter of "Contemporary Orthodontics, Seventh Edition" by Henry W. Fields Jr., Brent E. Larson, David M. Sarver, and William R. Proffit. It includes the title page, copyright and legal notices, information about the eBook access code, a list of contributors, the preface, acknowledgments, and a detailed table of contents. The preface explains that this edition updates the classic orthodontic textbook nearly 40 years after the first edition, noting the passing of William Proffit and the addition of new contributors covering topics such as artificial intelligence, data evaluation, obstructive sleep apnea, clear tray aligners, skeletal anchorage, and 3D orthognathic surgery planning. The table of contents outlines seven sections covering the orthodontic problem, diagnosis and treatment planning, biomechanics and appliances, treatment in preadolescent children, growth modification, comprehensive treatment in the early permanent dentition, and treatment for adults.

structure.title: Section 1: The Orthodontic Problem
structure.summary: The partial document introduces Section 1, "The Orthodontic Problem," outlining key foundational questions about orthodontics, including the rationale for treatment, patient need, benefits, prevalence, growth and development, eruption of teeth, etiology, and evidence-based treatment decisions. It emphasizes that these questions must be addressed before diagnosis and treatment planning, and notes that answers are provided in chapters 1–5.

nodes.title: Malocclusion and Dentofacial Abnormalities in Contemporary Society
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the introduction to malocclusion and dentofacial abnormalities, including the chapter outline listing topics such as changing goals of orthodontic treatment, epidemiology, treatment need, and AI in orthodontics. The main content provided focuses on the historical development of orthodontics: ancient attempts at tooth correction, early orthodontic devices, the emergence of systematic texts in the 19th century (notably Norman Kingsley's work), the evolution from simple tooth alignment to concepts of occlusion, and Edward H. Angle's pivotal contributions—his classification of malocclusion and definition of normal occlusion based on molar relationships and the line of occlusion.

nodes.title: The Changing Goals of Orthodontic Treatment
nodes.summary: This partial document is from Chapter 1 of an orthodontics textbook, titled “Malocclusion and Dentofacial Abnormalities in Contemporary Society.” It covers the historical development and changing goals of orthodontic treatment, from early attempts at tooth alignment to Angle’s classification of normal occlusion and malocclusion, and the later shift toward the soft tissue paradigm, which prioritizes facial soft tissue proportions and esthetics over ideal dental occlusion. It also discusses the epidemiology of malocclusion in the United States, including data from national surveys such as NHANES III on incisor irregularity, midline diastema, posterior crossbite, overjet, and overbite. The document addresses why malocclusion is prevalent, who needs treatment, psychosocial and functional impacts, the relationship to injury and dental disease, and methods for generating and assessing evidence, including evidence-based selection, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, retrospective studies, and the emerging role of artificial intelligence in orthodontics. It concludes with topics on demand for treatment, epidemiologic estimates of treatment need, and who seeks treatment.

nodes.title: The Usual Orthodontic Problems: Epidemiology of Malocclusion
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the introductory concepts of malocclusion and dentofacial abnormalities in contemporary society. It discusses the evolving goals of orthodontic treatment, emphasizing the importance of soft tissue and facial aesthetics, functional occlusion, and minimizing temporomandibular joint injury. It describes a reversed treatment planning thought process that begins with soft tissue goals before determining dental and skeletal arrangements. The document then reviews the epidemiology of malocclusion, particularly using NHANES III data for the U.S. population, including measures such as incisor irregularity, midline diastema, posterior crossbite, overjet, and overbite/open bite. It presents prevalence findings by age and racial/ethnic groups, notes differences in Angle Class II and Class III malocclusion, and compares U.S. data with international patterns. Finally, it explores why malocclusion is so prevalent, including evolutionary reductions in tooth and jaw size, the transition from primitive to modern urbanized societies, changes in diet and masticatory function, and parallels with "diseases of civilization."

nodes.title: Why Is Malocclusion So Prevalent?
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the prevalence and etiology of malocclusion. It notes that while anteroposterior problems are common, vertical problems are less prevalent in Latinx populations. Based on survey data, only about 30% of American children have normal occlusion, with Class II malocclusion affecting 15-20% and Class III less than 5%. It highlights racial and ethnic differences, such as higher Class II prevalence in northern European Whites and higher Class III prevalence in Asian populations. The text then explores why malocclusion is now so prevalent, contrasting modern crowded dentition with well-aligned ancient skeletal remains. It attributes this to evolutionary reductions in jaw size and tooth number, as well as recent lifestyle changes, including softer diets and urbanization, which reduce masticatory function. The section concludes by introducing reasons for orthodontic treatment, citing social discrimination due to appearance and problems with oral function.

nodes.title: Who Needs Treatment?
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the prevalence and consequences of malocclusion and dentofacial abnormalities, including the need for orthodontic treatment due to psychosocial problems, impaired oral function, temporomandibular dysfunction, and increased risk of injury and dental disease. It discusses the association between malocclusion and social handicaps, quality of life, and self-esteem, as well as the limited evidence linking malocclusion to TMD, tooth decay, and periodontal disease. It also introduces the concept of evidence-based treatment in orthodontics, emphasizing the hierarchy of evidence—from expert opinion and case reports to randomized clinical trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses—and the importance of using reliable evidence to guide clinical decisions. Additionally, the text includes illustrations on evolutionary tooth size reduction, missing teeth, masticatory muscle activity, a fractured incisor case, and the evidence hierarchy.

nodes.title: Generating and Assessing Data
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the relationship between malocclusion and oral health, noting weak evidence linking malocclusion to periodontal disease and emphasizing that oral hygiene and plaque are more important determinants. It covers evidence-based orthodontic treatment, explaining the hierarchy of evidence quality from expert opinion to meta-analyses, the importance of randomized clinical trials, systematic reviews, clinical practice guidelines, and the need for control groups in retrospective studies. It also introduces artificial intelligence (AI) in orthodontics, including digital workflows, machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, deep learning), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and graph neural networks (GNNs) for tasks like landmark detection, segmentation, and crowding assessment. Finally, it addresses demand for treatment and epidemiologic estimates of orthodontic need, describing indices such as the PAR (Peer Assessment Rating) and ABO (American Board of Orthodontics) discrepancy index used to score malocclusion severity.

nodes.title: Demand for Treatment
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers the following main points:

- Advances in AI for orthodontics, including convolutional neural networks (CNN) for measuring crowding, graph neural networks (GNN) for 3D intraoral scan data, automated tooth segmentation, landmark identification, and quantification of tooth movement. These AI tools are seen as promising for improving diagnosis, treatment planning, and outcome assessment.

- Demand for orthodontic treatment and epidemiologic estimates of treatment need. It discusses indices for scoring malocclusion severity: the Peer Assessment Rating (PAR) system, the American Board of Orthodontics (ABO) discrepancy index, and the Index of Treatment Need (IOTN), which grades patients from "no need" to "treatment required" based on dental health and esthetic components.

- Data on treatment need and receipt among U.S. youths by racial/ethnic group, showing higher treatment rates among White youths, and the impact of socioeconomic status. It notes that family income strongly influences treatment rates, with nearly 5% of the lowest income group still receiving treatment.

- The psychosocial impact of dental appearance, citing a survey showing that many adults, especially low-income and young adults, feel their teeth affect job interviews, social interactions, and confidence. A large majority believe straight, bright teeth help them get ahead in life.

- The growing demand for adult orthodontic treatment over the decades, from 5% in the 1960s to over 25% by 2017, with older adults (40+) becoming a fast-growing subgroup.

- The concept of orthodontics as an "enhancement" technology, similar to other medical/dental enhancements, and the argument that improving quality of life justifies treatment even for milder malocclusions.

- Evidence that orthodontic treatment improves quality of life and self-esteem in children and adults, and that individuals with dentofacial deviations benefit socially from correction.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses orthodontics as an enhancement technology in contemporary society, similar to other medical and dental enhancements like tooth bleaching. It emphasizes that enhancement procedures, including orthodontic treatment, are increasingly accepted as appropriate and reimbursable care. The text addresses whether orthodontic treatment improves quality of life and self-esteem, citing studies showing benefits for children, adolescents, and adults across different populations, including social advantages such as perceived intelligence and employability. It concludes that individuals benefit socially from correcting dental and facial appearance that deviates from their group's norms. The document also notes that orthodontics has become more prominent in dentistry and that most patients feel they benefited from treatment, recognizing improvements in dental condition and psychological well-being. The section ends with a list of references.

nodes.title: Concepts of Growth and Development
nodes.summary: The partial document introduces a chapter on concepts of growth and development in dentistry. It outlines topics including growth patterns, variability, timing, methods for studying growth, genetic influences, skeletal growth, craniofacial complex development, theories of growth control, and behavioral development. The text emphasizes the importance of understanding craniofacial growth for dentists, distinguishes between growth (increase in size) and development (increase in complexity), and previews coverage of physical and psychosocial aspects relevant to dental and orthodontic practice.

nodes.title: Growth: Pattern, Variability, and Timing
nodes.summary: This portion of the chapter introduces foundational concepts of craniofacial growth and development. It begins by emphasizing the importance of understanding these processes for dentists, both for treating children and for interpreting adult conditions. Key definitions are provided: growth refers to increase in size or number, while development refers to increasing complexity and specialization. The discussion then covers three fundamental concepts: pattern (proportional changes in body and facial dimensions over time, including the cephalocaudal gradient), variability (normal variation versus abnormal growth, assessed via growth charts and percentile tracking), and timing (differences in biological maturation, illustrated by adolescent growth spurts and the use of developmental age). The section on methods for studying physical growth distinguishes measurement approaches (noninvasive, longitudinal) from experimental approaches (manipulative, often destructive). Specific measurement techniques are introduced, beginning with craniometry, the measurement of skulls from skeletal remains. The text also references several figures illustrating changes in body proportions, Scammon's curves of tissue growth, growth charts, and velocity curves for height and maturation.

nodes.title: Methods for Studying Physical Growth
nodes.summary: The partial document covers concepts of growth and development relevant to orthodontics. It discusses biological versus chronological age, methods for studying physical growth (including measurement approaches such as craniometry, anthropometry, cephalometric radiology, and three-dimensional imaging, as well as analysis of measurement data using cross-sectional and longitudinal studies, distance and velocity curves, and mathematical transformations), experimental approaches (vital staining, autoradiography, and implant radiography), genetic influences on growth, and the fundamental nature of skeletal growth (including hypertrophy, hyperplasia, extracellular matrix secretion, interstitial versus surface apposition, and the role of cartilage and ossification).

nodes.title: The Nature of Skeletal Growth
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key concepts of growth and development in orthodontics, focusing on genetic and cellular mechanisms. It discusses genetic regulation of craniofacial development, including tissue interactions (e.g., muscle-bone interplay in the mandible, tooth eruption signaling), and the identification of genetic mutations like primary failure of eruption. It then explains the nature of skeletal growth, detailing three cellular mechanisms (hypertrophy, hyperplasia, extracellular secretion), the distinction between interstitial growth in soft tissues and surface apposition in mineralized hard tissues, and the processes of endochondral and intramembranous ossification. It also describes the development of the chondrocranium, epiphyseal plates, mandibular condyle, and maxilla, and contrasts bone modeling (shape-changing) with remodeling (internal turnover). Finally, it introduces the division of the craniofacial complex into four growth areas—cranial vault, cranial base, nasomaxillary complex, and mandible—as a framework for understanding their sites, types, mechanisms, and determinants of growth.

nodes.title: Sites and Types of Growth in the Craniofacial Complex
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key concepts of bone growth and development, specifically distinguishing between modeling (changes in bone size and shape) and remodeling (internal turnover without shape change). It then details the sites and types of growth in the craniofacial complex, including the cranial vault (intramembranous ossification at sutures), cranial base (endochondral ossification with synchondroses), maxilla/nasomaxillary complex (sutural apposition and surface modeling, with translation downward and forward), and mandible (condylar cartilage and posterior ramus apposition with anterior resorption). It also discusses growth of facial soft tissues, particularly the lips (trailing then catching up during adolescence) and nose (cartilage and soft tissue growth after age 10), and introduces three major theories of growth control.

nodes.title: Theories of Growth Control
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key concepts of craniofacial growth and development, including theories of growth control (bone, cartilage, and soft tissue/functional matrix theories), the distinction between growth sites and growth centers, and evidence from transplantation and removal experiments. It discusses the role of cartilage in mandibular and maxillary growth, particularly the mandibular condyle and nasal septum, and examines the functional matrix theory, which emphasizes soft tissue as the primary determinant of skeletal growth. The text also covers distraction osteogenesis as a method for inducing bone growth and correcting deficiencies. Additionally, it addresses cognitive, social, emotional, and behavioral development in dentistry, focusing on Piaget’s stages of cognitive development and their implications for communicating with child and adolescent orthodontic patients.

nodes.title: Cognitive, Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Development in Dentistry
nodes.summary: The partial document covers concepts of growth and development relevant to dentistry, focusing on cognitive, social, emotional, and behavioral development in pediatric and adolescent orthodontic patients. It discusses the interplay between genetic and environmental factors in physical growth and learned versus instinctual behavior, noting that human behavior is largely learned. It outlines Piaget’s stages of cognitive development—the concrete operational stage (ages 7–11) and the formal operational stage (from about age 11)—and explains how these stages affect communication and patient compliance, emphasizing the need for concrete instructions for younger children and more adult-like communication for adolescents. The text also addresses adolescent motivation, peer influence, and the importance of understanding the patient’s perceived reality, illustrated by a clinical case (Beth). Finally, it introduces mechanisms of learning—classical conditioning, operant conditioning, and observational learning—with a detailed explanation of classical conditioning (Pavlov’s experiments) and its application to dental anxiety, such as the association of white coats with pain and the potential benefit of a distinct dental office environment.

nodes.title: Learning and the Development of Behavior
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses concepts of growth and development related to patient behavior in orthodontic and dental settings. It begins with a case example of a teenage patient, Beth, whose concerns about wearing a removable partial denture were addressed by helping her reassess her peers' reactions, illustrating the dentist's role in guiding adolescents toward realistic evaluation of social situations. The text then introduces learning and behavior development, explaining that learning occurs through three mechanisms: classical conditioning (learning by association), operant conditioning (learning by consequences), and observational learning (modeling). Classical conditioning is described using Pavlov's experiments and applied to dental anxiety, such as associating white coats with pain. Operant conditioning covers positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, omission (negative punishment), and positive punishment, with examples relevant to dental visits and treatment adherence. Observational learning emphasizes how children acquire behaviors by imitating role models, including parents, siblings, and peers, and discusses the benefits of open treatment areas. Finally, the document addresses behavior management in orthodontic treatment, highlighting the practical use of reinforcement techniques and praise to encourage cooperative behavior in patients.

nodes.title: Behavior Management in Orthodontic Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers learning and behavior management principles in orthodontic treatment, and management of patients with neurodevelopmental, psychiatric, and gender-diverse conditions. Key points include: operant conditioning (punishment vs. positive/negative reinforcement) and observational learning (modeling) as frameworks for shaping patient behavior; practical applications of reinforcement, including praise, tangible rewards, timing, and managing between-visit compliance; limitations of omission and punishment, with voice control as a mild punitive technique; a 2022 meta-analysis indicating no single behavior management technique is superior, supporting clinician flexibility. The document then addresses orthodontic treatment for patients with intellectual disabilities, autism spectrum disorder (including sensory accommodations and desensitization), and ADHD (focusing on adherence and parental support), and concludes with considerations for gender-diverse individuals, including gender identity disclosure and treatment compromises to align with patient aesthetic goals.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document covers two main areas: first, an orthodontic section on working with gender-diverse patients, emphasizing the importance of sensitive communication, direct questions about gender identity, and potential treatment compromises to align with a patient’s aesthetic goals. Second, it introduces concepts of growth and development, focusing on late fetal development, birth, the neonatal line in teeth, and the mandible’s relative deficiency at birth.

nodes.title: Early Stages of Development
nodes.summary: The partial document covers a chapter outline and the beginning section on late fetal development and birth. It details fetal growth in the third trimester, the early development of primary teeth and first permanent molars, the adaptation of the fetal head shape for birth through fontanelles, and the normal mandibular deficiency in newborns. It also discusses the birth process as a growth interruption, resulting in the neonatal line in enamel and potential enamel disturbances.

nodes.title: Late Fetal Development and Birth
nodes.summary: The partial document covers Chapter 3, "Early Stages of Development," focusing on late fetal development, birth, and early childhood physical growth. It discusses fetal growth during the third trimester, dental development starting before birth, and the adaptations that facilitate birth, including head distortion due to fontanelles and mandibular deficiency. It also explains the impact of birth as a growth disturbance, resulting in the neonatal line in primary teeth. The document then addresses physical development in the preschool years, highlighting influences such as premature birth (low birth weight) and chronic illness on growth. Additionally, it includes a table on the chronology of primary tooth development and outlines topics for later sections, including maturation of oral function, eruption of primary and permanent teeth, and space relationships in dental replacement.

nodes.title: Infancy and Early Childhood: The Primary Dentition Years
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the early stages of human development, focusing on physical growth, factors influencing development, and oral maturation. Key topics include: the impact of birth and illnesses on tooth enamel formation; physical growth patterns in infancy and early childhood; influences such as premature birth/low birth weight, chronic illness, nutritional status, and secular trends in growth and maturation; maturation of oral functions including respiration, suckling, swallowing, chewing, and speech development; the eruption timeline and sequence of primary teeth, including primate spaces and natal teeth; and physical development in late childhood, including assessment of skeletal age via hand-wrist radiographs.

nodes.title: Late Childhood: The Mixed Dentition Years
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key topics in early orthodontic development, including: differences between juvenile and adult chewing patterns; eruption of primary teeth, including natal teeth, eruption timing/sequence, and primate spaces; physical development in late childhood (mixed dentition years); assessment of skeletal age using hand-wrist radiographs and cervical vertebral maturation (CVM), including their reliability and correlation with chronologic age; eruption of permanent teeth, with detailed discussion of preemergent eruption (bone resorption, propulsive mechanisms, cleidocranial dysplasia, primary failure of eruption, theories of eruption control) and postemergent eruption (postemergent spurt, circadian rhythms, juvenile and adult occlusal equilibrium, supereruption, ankylosis); eruption sequence and timing used to determine dental age from ages 6 to 15; space relationships in incisor replacement, including incisor liability, transitional crowding, sources of additional space, and the "ugly duckling" stage; and space relationships in replacement of canines and primary molars, including leeway space, E space, mesial molar shift, and transitions from flush terminal plane, distal step, or mesial step relationships to permanent molar occlusion.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the transition from primary to permanent molar relationships, focusing on how different terminal plane relationships (distal step, flush terminal plane, mesial step) can evolve into Class I, Class II, or Class III relationships depending on the amount and direction of mandibular growth and tooth shifting. It emphasizes that mandibular growth, not the movement of permanent molars when primary second molars are lost, is the key determinant. The text also includes a figure legend illustrating occlusal relationships and a list of references on topics such as growth, tooth eruption, and developmental milestones.

nodes.title: Later Stages of Development
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the later stages of dentofacial development, focusing on adolescence and early permanent dentition. It outlines key topics such as the initiation and timing of puberty, growth patterns of the dentofacial complex, jaw rotation, tooth eruption interactions, and aging changes in adults, including facial soft tissues, alignment, occlusion, and dental structures. The text specifically details the biological onset of adolescence, emphasizing the role of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, GnRH secretion, pituitary gonadotropins, and sex hormones in triggering puberty and associated physical changes relevant to orthodontic treatment.

nodes.title: Adolescence: The Early Permanent Dentition Years
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the later stages of craniofacial development, focusing on adolescence and the early permanent dentition years. It discusses the initiation of puberty, emphasizing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, hormonal regulation, and the role of GnRH and sex hormones. It details the timing of puberty, including differences between girls and boys, Tanner stages of sexual development, factors affecting maturation, and implications for orthodontic treatment timing. The document also addresses growth patterns in the dentofacial complex, including dimensional changes in the nasomaxillary complex and mandible, jaw rotation, interactions between jaw growth and tooth eruption, and maturational and aging changes affecting facial soft tissues, occlusion, and dental structures.

nodes.title: Growth Patterns in the Dentofacial Complex
nodes.summary: The partial document covers later stages of dentofacial development, focusing on growth patterns. It explains the nasomaxillary complex growth via passive displacement and active sutural growth, with surface modeling adding or removing bone. Nasal growth is faster than maxillary growth, especially during adolescence. Mandibular growth includes chin prominence changes and variability due to glenoid fossa movement. It describes the timing of growth in width, length, and height, noting width completes first, then length, then height. The document also details jaw rotation during growth, based on implant studies, distinguishing internal, external, and total rotation. It discusses short-face and long-face rotational patterns and their effects on malocclusion, as well as the interaction between jaw rotation and tooth eruption.

nodes.title: Interaction Between Jaw Rotation and Tooth Eruption
nodes.summary: The partial document covers jaw rotation patterns in orthodontics, distinguishing between short-face and long-face individuals and their effects on mandibular growth, tooth eruption, and malocclusion. It explains how internal and external rotation of the mandible influence facial structure, condylar growth direction, palatal plane orientation, and dental positioning, leading to deep bite or open bite tendencies. It also discusses the interaction between jaw rotation and tooth eruption, including effects on incisor position and arch length. Additionally, it covers maturational and aging changes in facial growth, citing Behrents' study showing continued adult facial growth, jaw rotation, and sex-specific differences in skeletal changes.

nodes.title: Maturational and Aging Changes
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the later stages of craniofacial development, focusing on maturational and aging changes in the face and jaws. It describes how jaw rotation and tooth eruption interact to influence tooth positioning in individuals with vertical facial disproportions. Key findings from Behrents’s longitudinal study demonstrate that facial growth continues well into adulthood, with sex-specific differences: males tend to exhibit forward jaw rotation and anterior growth, while females show more vertical and backward changes. The document also details age-related changes in facial soft tissues, including nose elongation, chin augmentation, lip lengthening and thinning, and reduced upper incisor exposure, which have important implications for orthodontic treatment planning. It discusses the development of late mandibular incisor crowding, evaluating three main theories: lack of attrition, pressure from third molars, and late mandibular growth—the latter being supported by implant studies showing lingual displacement of lower incisors. Finally, aging changes in teeth and supporting structures are addressed, including pulp chamber narrowing due to continued dentin deposition, gingival attachment levels related to active eruption rather than passive migration, and reduced occlusal wear in modern diets.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document includes content from two chapters of an orthodontics textbook. From Chapter 4, it discusses age-related changes in gingival and periodontal tissues, clarifies that “passive eruption” does not occur in healthy gingiva, and contrasts severe dental wear from coarse ancient diets with modern wear typically indicating bruxism. This section ends with a long reference list. From Chapter 5, it provides an outline of topics on the etiology of orthodontic problems and introduces key concepts: malocclusion as a developmental deviation, definitions of malformation versus deformation, hereditary versus congenital disorders, stages of fetal development, and the epidemiological finding that only about 5% of malocclusions have a specific known cause while most arise from complex genetic and environmental interactions.

nodes.title: The Etiology of Orthodontic Problems
nodes.summary: The partial document is from a chapter on the etiology of orthodontic problems. It introduces malocclusion as a developmental condition caused by deviations from normal development, ranging from mild to severe. It defines key terminology: malformation (intrinsic developmental anomaly) versus deformation (mechanical distortion), and distinguishes hereditary, congenital, and genetic disorders. It outlines three stages of fetal development and notes that most craniofacial defects arise during the embryonic period (3–8 weeks). Statistics show that about two-thirds of the US population has some malocclusion, but only 5% have a known specific cause. The chapter then begins discussing specific causes, starting with disturbances in embryologic development, including teratogens (e.g., alcohol, Accutane, Zika virus) and their effects on craniofacial development. It highlights the role of neural crest cells and neurocristopathies in facial formation, citing examples like thalidomide and isotretinoin. The text also lists common craniofacial anomalies such as cleft lip/palate, Treacher Collins, craniosynostosis, hemifacial microsomia, microcephaly, and microtia.

nodes.title: Specific Causes of Malocclusion
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the etiology of orthodontic problems, focusing on known specific causes, hereditary/genetic influences, and environmental influences. It begins with disturbances in embryologic development, including teratogens, neural crest cell abnormalities, fetal alcohol syndrome, and conditions such as cleft lip and palate, Treacher Collins syndrome, craniofacial microsomia, craniosynostosis, microcephaly, and microtia. It then discusses growth disturbances in the fetal and perinatal period, including intrauterine molding, birth trauma, Pierre Robin sequence, childhood jaw fractures, muscle dysfunction, and adolescent/early adult conditions such as hemimandibular hypertrophy and acromegaly. Dental development disturbances are also covered, including congenitally missing teeth, malformed and supernumerary teeth, and traumatic tooth displacement. The text also introduces genetic influences on skeletal and dental malocclusion.

nodes.title: Genetic Influences
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the etiology of orthodontic problems, focusing on several key causes. It covers supernumerary teeth, their potential to disrupt occlusion, their common location in the maxillary anterior region, and their association with conditions like cleidocranial dysplasia and ectodermal dysplasia. It also describes the effects of traumatic displacement of primary teeth on permanent tooth development, including enamel defects and root dilaceration, as well as treatment considerations. Genetic influences on malocclusion are examined in depth, including hereditary jaw and tooth size discrepancies, the Hapsburg jaw, historical dog-breeding experiments by Stockard, the role of achondroplasia, and population studies such as those in Hawaii. The text reviews evidence from twin and family studies on heritability of craniofacial and dental characteristics, noting strong genetic influence on skeletal features and mandibular prognathism, while dental variations are more environmentally influenced. Finally, the document introduces environmental influences and equilibrium considerations, explaining how forces from mastication, swallowing, and speaking are balanced, and how prolonged or altered forces—such as orthodontic appliances or scarring—can affect tooth position and dental arch form.

nodes.title: Environmental Influences
nodes.summary:
This partial document covers the etiology of orthodontic problems, focusing on the roles of heredity and environment. Key points include:

- **Heredity vs. Environment**: Heritability of craniofacial skeletal characteristics is high, while dental/occlusal characteristics are more environmentally determined. Mandibular prognathism has a significant hereditary component, possibly involving a major gene, but Class III malocclusion comprises diverse phenotypes.
- **Equilibrium Theory**: Tooth position is determined by a balance of sustained, light forces (lips, cheeks, tongue at rest) rather than heavy, short-duration forces (mastication, swallowing). Alterations in resting pressures can move teeth.
- **Masticatory Function**: Chewing force and dietary consistency may affect jaw/dental arch size, but evidence is unclear. Biting force differences in long-face vs normal-face individuals appear to be an effect of growth pattern, not a cause.
- **Sucking and Habits**: Prolonged thumb or pacifier sucking can cause flared incisors, open bite, and narrow maxillary arch, but effects are reversible if the habit stops early.
- **Tongue Thrusting**: Tongue thrust swallow is usually a transitional stage or an adaptation to open bite, not a primary cause of malocclusion. Sustained tongue resting posture, however, can affect tooth position.
- **Respiratory Pattern and Mouth Breathing**: Total nasal obstruction can alter facial growth; partial obstruction shows only modest correlations with long-face morphology. Most long-face patients are not primarily mouth breathers.
- **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)**: OSA is not strongly linked to typical orthodontic morphology; orthodontic extractions and headgear do not worsen airway dimensions.
- **Contemporary Perspective**: Modern understanding rejects both purely genetic and purely functional explanations; malocclusion results from multiple interacting genetic and environmental factors, and much remains unknown.

nodes.title: Etiology in Contemporary Perspective
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the lack of evidence linking orthodontic extractions or headgear treatment to obstructive sleep apnea or negative upper airway changes, noting minimal long-term skeletal effects and primarily dentoalveolar changes. It also discusses the evolving understanding of malocclusion etiology, from early beliefs in environmental causes, to genetic determinism, to a modern balanced view acknowledging complex interacting factors.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document covers two main areas: the orthodontic problem and diagnosis/treatment planning. It first discusses evidence on whether orthodontic treatments like headgear or premolar extractions affect airway dimensions or obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), concluding that current research shows no significant negative effects on airway or OSA prevalence. It then reviews evolving theories on the etiology of malocclusion, from early beliefs in environmental causes to heredity, and finally to a contemporary balanced view recognizing multiple interacting factors with no simple explanation. The document then transitions to Section 2, outlining the principles of orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning: collecting a patient database, formulating a problem list, setting prioritized treatment goals, and evaluating timing, complexity, predictability, and patient expectations.

structure.title: Section 2: Diagnosis and Treatment Planning
structure.summary: The partial document introduces the problem-oriented approach to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It emphasizes that diagnosis requires gathering a comprehensive patient database and formulating a problem list that includes both patient perceptions and doctor’s observations, distinguishing pathologic from developmental problems. Treatment planning involves setting prioritized goals, considering alternative solutions, and creating a strategy that maximizes patient benefit. The document contrasts diagnosis (aimed at factual truth) with treatment planning (requiring clinical wisdom and judgment). It then discusses key issues in treatment planning: timing, treatment complexity, predictability/success of methods, and the necessity of interactive patient involvement. A logical sequence for treatment planning is provided. The text also includes the beginning of Chapter 6, outlining the problem-oriented diagnostic process, the need for a broad overview to avoid overlooking problems, and the three major sources of diagnostic data: interview, clinical examination, and diagnostic records.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Diagnosis: The Problem-Oriented Approach
nodes.summary: The partial document introduces the problem-oriented approach to orthodontic diagnosis, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive patient evaluation rather than focusing solely on dental occlusion. It outlines three major sources of diagnostic information: interview data, clinical examination, and diagnostic records. The text then details the questionnaire and interview process, highlighting the importance of establishing the patient's chief concern and gathering medical/dental history, as well as social and behavioral factors. A sample patient questionnaire is included to illustrate how to elicit patient and parent concerns about dental and facial appearance, growth expectations, and treatment motivations. The chief concern is stressed as a critical component that must be identified and addressed for successful treatment planning.

nodes.title: Questionnaire and Interview
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key components of orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, emphasizing a problem-oriented approach. It begins with the goals of the patient interview and questionnaire, focusing on identifying the chief concern, medical/dental history, and patient motivation and expectations. A detailed medical/dental history form is discussed, with special attention to trauma, long-term medications, cancer treatment effects, bisphosphonates, and the importance of screening for sleep-disordered breathing using tools like the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ) and STOP-Bang questionnaire. White spot lesions and oral hygiene risks are also addressed. The social and behavioral evaluation section highlights internal vs. external motivation, patient expectations, cooperation, and the need for assent in minors. Finally, the clinical evaluation section covers assessment of statural and sexual maturation, growth status, and the use of growth records.

nodes.title: Clinical Evaluation
nodes.summary: The partial document covers factors influencing orthodontic treatment, including types of patient motivation (external vs. internal), the importance of internal motivation for cooperation, and the need to assess patient expectations, especially for cosmetic issues. It discusses cooperation challenges in children and the role of parenting style, the necessity of patient assent for minors, and the goals of clinical evaluation—specifically assessing statural and sexual maturation to guide growth modification and treatment timing.

nodes.title: CHAPTER 6 Orthodontic Diagnosis: The Problem-Oriented Approach
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses factors influencing orthodontic treatment, including patient motivation (external vs. internal), the importance of realistic expectations, cooperation and parenting style, and the need for patient assent. It also introduces the goals of the clinical examination, focusing on evaluating growth, dental relationships, and jaw function, with emphasis on assessing statural and sexual maturation to time treatment appropriately.

nodes.title: Clinical Evaluation
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses patient motivation for orthodontic treatment, distinguishing between external and internal motivation, and emphasizes the importance of internal motivation for cooperation. It covers patient expectations, especially regarding cosmetic outcomes, and the risks of unrealistic expectations. Cooperation is examined in relation to parenting style and patient receptiveness. Legal consent and child assent are addressed. The document then introduces the clinical evaluation section, covering the goals of the orthodontic examination, with a focus on evaluating statural growth and sexual maturation, including methods like height measurement with a stadiometer and the relationship between growth status and treatment timing.

nodes.title: Statural and Sexual Maturation Evaluation
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses factors influencing orthodontic treatment motivation (external vs. internal), the importance of patient expectations and realistic goals, cooperation factors in children including parenting style, and legal consent/assent for minors. It then introduces the clinical evaluation, focusing on two goals: assessing growth, oral health, and dental relationships, and determining needed diagnostic records. Specific attention is given to statural and sexual maturation evaluation (using height measurements, Tanner stages, and growth charts) and oral health assessment (controlling caries and periodontal disease, counting teeth, documenting hygiene, caries risk assessment, and probing for bleeding/inflammation).

nodes.title: Oral Health
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key components of orthodontic diagnosis, including: assessment of facial growth using serial cephalometric radiographs; evaluation of oral hard and soft tissue health prior to treatment, with emphasis on controlling caries, periodontal disease, and other pathologies; use of the ADA Caries Risk Assessment form to systematically evaluate caries risk; periodontal examination to detect active disease, bleeding on probing, and mucogingival problems; consideration of developmental tooth defects such as Molar Incisor Hypomineralization; and documentation of dental relationships including molar and canine classification, overbite, overjet, crossbite, and midline discrepancies. It also includes a table on adolescent growth stages (Tanner stages) and figures illustrating oral hygiene variations, aggressive periodontitis, and inadequate attached gingiva.

nodes.title: Dental Relationships—Intra and Interarch
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key considerations in orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, focusing on periodontal health, developmental tooth defects, dental relationships, and occlusal function. It highlights the importance of identifying aggressive juvenile periodontitis before treatment, the risk of gingival stripping with inadequate attached gingiva, and the need to account for enamel defects like Molar Incisor Hypomineralization (MIH). It emphasizes thorough clinical examination of intra-arch and interarch relationships, including molar/canine classification, overbite, overjet, crossbites, CR-CO shifts, and midline discrepancies. Additionally, it discusses evaluating jaw and occlusal function, including mastication, speech, and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) issues, and the impact of neuromuscular conditions on treatment outcomes.

nodes.title: Jaw and Occlusal Function
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers aspects of orthodontic diagnosis, including:

- Identification and differentiation of enamel defects, such as fluorosis, local hypoplastic defects from trauma or primary tooth pulpal degeneration, and molar incisor hypomineralization.
- Documentation of occlusal characteristics, including overbite, overjet, anterior and posterior crossbites, centric relation–centric occlusion shifts, and midline relationships.
- Evaluation of jaw and occlusal function, focusing on mastication, swallowing, speech, and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) assessment.
- Discussion of speech difficulties related to specific malocclusions and the limited role of orthodontics in resolving speech problems.
- Emphasis on TMJ screening, including range of motion, tenderness, joint sounds, and deviations on opening.
- Introduction to the soft-tissue paradigm in orthodontic diagnosis, tracing its historical roots to Norman Kingsley and Edward Angle.

nodes.title: Facial and Dental Appearance: The Evolution To Today’s Soft-Tissue Paradigm
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the limited role of swallowing and oral gymnastic tests in orthodontic diagnosis, and the relationship between speech problems and malocclusion—noting that orthodontic treatment rarely resolves speech issues and that specific speech-malocclusion associations should be evaluated by specialists. It then discusses jaw function and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) examination, emphasizing maximum opening, mandibular translation, palpation, and detection of shifts; in children, functional mandibular shifts can create apparent unilateral crossbites or pseudo–class III malocclusion. Occlusal interferences become more significant near the end of orthodontic treatment. The document also traces the evolution of orthodontic diagnosis from occlusion-focused to a soft-tissue paradigm, highlighting contributions from Kingsley, Angle, and the later influence of cephalometrics, leading to today’s facial and smile focus. Finally, it presents eye-tracking and social judgment studies showing how background facial attractiveness interacts with dental attractiveness, affecting how people perceive teeth and how dental esthetics influence judgments of intelligence, social class, and popularity differently for males and females.

nodes.title: Effect of Background Facial Attractiveness on Perceptions of Dental Esthetics
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the shift in orthodontic diagnosis from a purely occlusion-focused approach to a greater emphasis on facial and smile esthetics, influenced by advances in cephalometry and interdisciplinary treatment. It discusses research on how background facial attractiveness affects perceptions of dental esthetics, using eye-tracking studies and the IOTN-AC index to quantify gaze patterns and the impact of teeth on overall facial attractiveness. It highlights gender differences in how dental attractiveness influences social, intellectual, and integrity judgments. The document then introduces a systematic three-step examination of facial and dental appearance: macroesthetics (facial proportions in three planes), mini-esthetics (dentition in relation to the face, including smile and gingival display), and microesthetics (tooth proportions, gingival contours, and tooth shade). It also explains facial form analysis and the importance of evaluating facial proportions rather than esthetics alone.

nodes.title: Systematic Examination of Facial and Dental Appearance
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the systematic examination of facial and dental appearance in three steps: macroesthetics (facial proportions in all three planes), mini-esthetics (dentition in relation to the face), and microesthetics (teeth in relation to one another). It emphasizes the importance of evaluating facial proportions over esthetics alone, noting that facial attractiveness affects dental judgments and that disproportionate faces cause psychosocial issues. It introduces facial form analysis as a clinical, non-radiographic evaluation of the face in frontal, antero-posterior, and vertical dimensions, considering patient maturity. The text also highlights key assessment points, such as facial symmetry, vertical proportions, maxillary/mandibular positioning, and lip protrusion relative to reference lines.

nodes.title: Macroesthetics: Facial Proportions
nodes.summary: The document discusses the systematic examination of facial and dental appearance in three steps: macroesthetics (facial proportions in all three planes), mini-esthetics (dentition in relation to the face, including smile arc, gingival display, and buccal corridors), and microesthetics (teeth in relation to one another, such as tooth proportions, gingival contours, and embrasures). It emphasizes the importance of evaluating facial proportions over esthetics alone, noting that cultural factors influence attractiveness but disproportionate faces cause psychosocial issues. The section introduces facial form analysis, a clinical examination of frontal, antero-posterior, and vertical dimensions without radiography, using landmarks like the Nasion Perpendicular, E-line, and lip protrusion, while considering patient maturity.

nodes.title: Facial Esthetics Versus Facial Proportions
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the systematic examination of facial and dental appearance in three steps: macroesthetics (facial proportions in all three planes), mini-esthetics (dentition in relation to the face, including smile display and gingival exposure), and microesthetics (teeth in relation to one another, such as tooth proportions and gingival contours). It emphasizes the importance of assessing facial attractiveness alongside dental attractiveness, distinguishes facial esthetics from facial proportions, and introduces facial form analysis as a clinical, non-radiographic evaluation of frontal, anteroposterior, and vertical dimensions. The text also notes that facial proportions, rather than beauty per se, are key to psychosocial outcomes, and that patient maturity and cultural factors influence expectations.

nodes.title: Facial Form Analysis
nodes.summary: The partial document focuses on orthodontic diagnosis, specifically the systematic evaluation of facial and dental appearance. It outlines a three-step examination: macroesthetics (facial proportions in all three planes), mini-esthetics (the dentition in relation to the face, including smile arc, gingival display, and buccal corridors), and microesthetics (the teeth in relation to one another, such as tooth proportions, gingival contours, and embrasures). It emphasizes that facial attractiveness influences judgments of dental esthetics and that proportionate facial features are generally acceptable even if not beautiful. The text introduces the facial form analysis as the macroesthetic evaluation, using frontal, profile, and vertical assessments without radiography. It details the frontal examination, including bilateral symmetry, facial fifths, eye and mouth widths, and detection of possible syndromes or craniofacial anomalies. A checklist for the facial form analysis is provided, covering frontal at rest, frontal smile, frontal widths, profile, vertical lower face, nose, lips, and throat form. The section also notes the historical use of anthropometric measurements and the importance of considering patient maturity when assessing facial form.

nodes.title: Frontal Examination
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the clinical extraoral facial examination in orthodontic diagnosis, emphasizing the importance of projecting future adolescent and adult esthetics. It provides a systematic checklist for facial form analysis, including frontal and profile evaluations. Key points include: assessing frontal proportions and symmetry, identifying potential syndromes (e.g., low-set ears, hypertelorism), distinguishing normal asymmetry from significant deviations, and using anthropometric measurements for facial proportions. The text discusses vertical facial thirds and the facial index, noting ethnic and gender variations. Profile analysis involves evaluating facial form in natural head position, determining skeletal jaw relationships (convex/concave profiles), and assessing maxillary and mandibular contributions to malocclusions using Nasion Perpendicular and Frankfort Horizontal references. It also addresses causes of excessive gingival display and the importance of considering soft tissue proportions in treatment planning.

nodes.title: Profile Analysis
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic diagnosis through facial profile analysis and introduces mini-esthetic examination. It details a four-step profile evaluation: (1) establishing overall facial form using natural head position and profile convexity/concavity to identify skeletal class II or III relationships; (2) determining maxillary and mandibular contributions to skeletal malocclusions via Frankfort Horizontal and Nasion Perpendicular references, including assessment of throat form; (3) evaluating lip posture and incisor prominence, focusing on lip competence, bimaxillary dentoalveolar protrusion, ethnic/age variations, and clinical guidelines such as the E-line and nasolabial angle; and (4) reevaluating vertical facial proportions and mandibular plane angle. The text also emphasizes the importance of preserving positive facial attributes during treatment and briefly introduces mini-esthetics, covering tooth-lip relationships, midlines, gingival display, occlusal cant, buccal corridors, and smile arc.

nodes.title: Mini-esthetics: Tooth-Lip Relationships and Smile Analysis
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic diagnostic evaluation of facial and dental esthetics, organized into macroesthetics, mini-esthetics, and microesthetics. It discusses lip prominence and incisor position relative to facial profile, including racial/ethnic and age variations, the E-line, nasolabial angle, and vertical facial proportions with mandibular plane angle assessment. It emphasizes evaluating both positive and negative attributes to avoid harming facial balance during treatment. Mini-esthetics focuses on tooth-lip relationships and smile analysis: dental midlines and angulation, gingival display (with etiologies for gummy smile), transverse occlusal cant, buccal corridors, smile arc (including consonant and nonconsonant forms), and smile asymmetries. Microesthetics addresses close-up dental appearance: tooth width proportions and the golden proportion, height-width relationships of incisors, connectors and embrasures, and black triangles from deficient interdental papillae. The text also highlights that smile esthetics are influenced by dynamic factors and should be assessed in full-face context.

nodes.title: Microesthetics: Close-up Dental Appearance
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses key factors in smile esthetics and orthodontic treatment planning. It emphasizes the smile arc as the most critical factor in smile esthetics, and outlines causes of smile asymmetries, including skeletal, dental, and soft tissue factors. It then covers microesthetic considerations for close-up dental appearance, such as tooth proportions (including the golden proportion for width relationships), height-width relationships of teeth, and the significance of connectors and embrasures. It also addresses problems like black triangles due to short interdental papillae, and includes checklists of etiologies for smile arc issues and smile asymmetry. Overall, it highlights the importance of evaluating these esthetic details for optimal orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning.

nodes.title: Tooth Proportions
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses key factors in smile esthetics for orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It emphasizes that the smile arc is a critical determinant of smile attractiveness. It then covers causes of smile asymmetries, including skeletal, dental, and soft tissue factors. The text also addresses microesthetic considerations of dental appearance, such as tooth proportions (including the golden proportion for width relationships), height-to-width ratios of teeth, and the importance of connectors and embrasures in smile design. Additionally, it mentions black triangles from short interdental papillae and includes checklists of etiologies for smile arc problems and smile asymmetry.

nodes.title: Connectors and Embrasures
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses diagnosis and treatment planning for smile esthetics, focusing on key factors that influence smile appearance. It highlights the smile arc as the most critical factor, then addresses causes of smile asymmetries (e.g., skeletal, dental, soft tissue, trauma). It also covers microesthetic considerations: tooth proportions (including the "golden proportion" for width relationships), height-width relationships of teeth, connectors and embrasures, and problems like black triangles from short interdental papillae. Additionally, it includes checklists of etiologies for smile arc issues and smile asymmetry.

nodes.title: Embrasures: Black Triangles
nodes.summary: The partial document focuses on smile esthetics and microesthetic factors in orthodontic diagnosis. Key points include the smile arc as the most important factor, various causes of smile asymmetries, and detailed dental appearance elements: tooth width relationships (golden proportion of 62%), height-width proportions of anterior teeth, connectors and embrasures, black triangles from short interdental papillae, and gingival heights, shape, contour, and color. It emphasizes integrating these factors into orthodontic problem lists and treatment planning.

nodes.title: Gingival Heights, Shape, Contour, and Color
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses microesthetic elements of a smile in orthodontic diagnosis, focusing on dental and gingival details. Key points include: management of black triangles after orthodontic alignment, especially in adults with prior crowding; ideal gingival height relationships (central incisor highest, lateral incisor ~1.5 mm lower, canine at central level); gingival shape and the location of the gingival zenith; undesirable gingival color variations from inflammation or patchy pigmentation; and tooth shade/color changes with aging, including the normal tonal gradation from brighter central incisors to darker canines. It also references illustrations of the golden proportion for tooth widths and height-width ratios for central incisors.

nodes.title: Tooth Shade and Color
nodes.summary: The partial document covers aspects of orthodontic diagnosis related to esthetic considerations and diagnostic records. It discusses gingival appearance issues, including black triangles and unattractive gingival color variations such as inflammation and patchy pigmentation. It then addresses tooth shade and color changes with aging, explaining the role of secondary dentin and enamel thinning, and introduces the concept of tonal gradation in a natural smile. The text also notes patient awareness of tooth bleaching and the need to include shade concerns in the treatment plan, while acknowledging that restorations will not lighten with bleaching. The document then transitions to diagnostic records, outlining the purposes and categories of orthodontic records, and detailing records for assessing the health of teeth and oral structures, including standard intraoral photographs and the use of panoramic radiographs, with supplementary periapical or occlusal radiographs as needed, and considerations for adult pretreatment radiographs.

nodes.title: Diagnostic Records
key_items: Records for Health of Teeth and Oral Structures
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses diagnosis and treatment planning, focusing on tooth bleaching considerations in orthodontic patients and the importance of including tooth color in the treatment plan. It then details diagnostic records: their purposes (documenting starting point and supplementing clinical exam), three categories (health of teeth/oral structures, alignment/occlusion, facial/jaw proportions), and the shift to digital imaging. Specific record types include standard intraoral photographs, panoramic radiographs (advantages: broader view, lower radiation, condyle screening), supplemental periapical/occlusal radiographs when needed, and indications for TMJ imaging. It also notes that restorations will not lighten with bleaching and may need replacement.

nodes.title: Diagnostic Records
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, focusing on diagnostic records and their analysis. It discusses the importance of tooth color/bleaching considerations in treatment planning, then details the types of diagnostic records needed: records for health of teeth and oral structures (intraoral photographs, panoramic radiographs, supplemental periapicals, and CBCT for impacted canines), dental records (impressions, physical vs. virtual casts, wax bites, and articulator mounting), and records for dentofacial proportions (cephalometric radiographs and facial photographs). A summary emphasizes minimal records and radiation safety guidelines. The document then explains analysis of diagnostic records, including dental cast analysis for symmetry, space analysis, and tooth-size (Bolton) analysis, followed by a comprehensive section on cephalometric analysis: its history, landmarks, development, reference lines (Frankfort plane, sella-nasion, natural head position), and specific analyses such as Steiner, Sassouni, Harvold, Wits, McNamara, and template analysis.

nodes.title: Template Analysis Techniques
nodes.summary: The partial document covers multiple aspects of orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It begins with a discussion of cephalometric measurement analyses, including the Harvold analysis (maxillary and mandibular length, lower face height), the WITS analysis (with caution about geometric idiosyncrasies affecting interpretation), and the McNamara analysis (maxillary/mandibular protrusion, incisor protrusion, lengths, lower face height). It then focuses on template analysis, explaining the concept of average composite tracings from growth studies (e.g., Michigan, Burlington, Bolton templates) and how superimposition of a patient’s tracing on age- and sex-matched templates can visually reveal skeletal and dental discrepancies, with steps for cranial base, maxillary, and mandibular superimposition. The document then describes serial cephalometric superimposition techniques for evaluating growth and treatment changes, specifying the anatomic registration areas for cranial base, maxillary, and mandibular superimpositions as recommended by the American Board of Orthodontics. Growth staging methods such as cervical vertebral maturation and hand-wrist radiographs are discussed, noting limitations and the superiority of serial cephalometric radiographs for determining growth completion. A seven-step methodology for cephalometric analysis in the digital age is outlined, emphasizing pathology screening, positioning error checks, landmark verification, awareness of geometric interpretation pitfalls, consistency of measurements, and assessment of facial proportionality. The text extensively covers three-dimensional imaging with cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), including basic concepts (voxels, resolution, field of view, radiation dose), orthodontic applications (impacted/ectopic teeth, resorption, facial asymmetry, orthognathic surgery, congenital deformities such as cleft lip/palate, dental trauma/transplantation, TMJ hard tissue issues), diagnostic scope and risks of overdiagnosis, evaluation of growth and treatment changes using voxel-based superimposition and color maps, and limitations of CBCT for OSA airway evaluation. Finally, it addresses orthodontic classification, presenting Angle’s classification (normal occlusion, Class I, II, III malocclusion) and the conceptual role of classification in reducing diagnostic data into a problem list and positive attributes to maintain.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Classification
nodes.summary: The partial document covers limitations of CBCT for OSA airway evaluation, noting poor reliability and lack of predictive value. It then discusses orthodontic classification systems, from Angle's original classification to the Ackerman-Proffit five-characteristics scheme, and modern additions such as the esthetic line of the dentition and pitch, roll, and yaw rotations. It details the step-by-step classification process: evaluation of facial proportions/esthetics, alignment and symmetry, transverse plane, anteroposterior plane, vertical plane, and concludes with development of a problem list.

nodes.title: Development of a Problem List
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic diagnosis with a focus on skeletal vertical problems, including deep bite and open bite relationships. It explains the role of cephalometric analysis in evaluating mandibular and palatal plane angles to identify skeletal deep bite or open bite tendencies, and emphasizes the importance of clinical evaluation of dentition to soft tissues. The document then details the development of a problem list, distinguishing pathologic problems from developmental abnormalities related to malocclusion, and advocates for quantitative or severity-based classification. It presents a case study of patient F.P., including interview data, clinical examination findings, radiographs, and a classified problem list covering facial esthetics, dental alignment, transverse relationships, anteroposterior relationships, and vertical relationships. The text concludes that a thorough diagnostic evaluation leads to a complete problem list before treatment planning begins, and includes references.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It begins with Chapter 6, "Orthodontic Diagnosis: The Problem-Oriented Approach," emphasizing the need for a thorough diagnostic evaluation that identifies and characterizes all problems. It includes a list of references supporting diagnostic methods and a boxed example (Box 6.5) showing a classified problem list for a patient (F.P.), using the Ackerman-Proffit classification to categorize facial/esthetic, dental alignment, transverse, anteroposterior, and vertical problems. The document then transitions to Chapter 7, "Orthodontic Treatment Planning: From Problem List to Specific Plan," outlining topics such as treatment planning concepts and goals, major planning issues, treatment possibilities, skeletal/dental considerations, comprehensive treatment planning steps, informed consent, special circumstances, sleep apnea treatment, and management of dentofacial/craniofacial anomalies. Initial text discusses that diagnosis is complete when a comprehensive problem list and positive attributes are developed, and treatment planning aims to set goals and design strategies that maximize benefit while minimizing cost and risk, with emphasis on prioritizing the patient's overall health (e.g., controlling periodontal disease before aligning teeth).

nodes.title: Orthodontic Treatment Planning: From Problem List to Specific Plan
nodes.summary: The partial document is a chapter on orthodontic treatment planning, outlining the process from problem list to a specific plan. It covers major planning issues such as patient input, predictability, and treatment possibilities, including dental crowding (expansion vs. extraction), skeletal problems, and mini-implant augmented treatment. It also addresses aesthetic considerations (macro, mini, and micro), comprehensive treatment planning steps, informed consent, and special circumstances like disease, injuries, and sleep apnea. Additionally, it lists common dentofacial anomalies and introduces the initial concept of treatment planning: setting goals and designing strategies that maximize patient benefit while minimizing cost and risk, with emphasis on prioritizing patient needs over solely orthodontic concerns.

nodes.title: Treatment Planning Concepts and Goals
nodes.summary: The partial document is from an orthodontic textbook chapter on treatment planning, covering the transition from a problem list to a specific treatment plan. It outlines key concepts and goals, emphasizes patient input and ethical considerations, and discusses major issues such as treatment predictability, complexity, and the choice between arch expansion and extraction for crowding. It also addresses skeletal problems with macro-esthetic considerations, mini-implant (TAD) augmented treatment, and micro-esthetic improvements for smile and tooth appearance. The text details steps in planning comprehensive treatment, setting priorities and goals, evaluating treatment possibilities, creating a detailed plan, and obtaining informed consent. It further covers treatment planning for special circumstances including dental and systemic diseases, injuries, and sleep apnea (in both children and adults), as well as common dentofacial and craniofacial anomalies like hemimandibular hypertrophy and cleft lip and palate.

nodes.title: Major Issues in Planning Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key concepts in orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It emphasizes that treatment plans should be developed collaboratively with the patient, focusing on "should we?" rather than "could we?" and using cost-benefit and risk-benefit analyses. It highlights the importance of avoiding both missed opportunities and excessive treatment. Major issues discussed include: the need for interactive patient input and informed consent; the role of predictability and complexity in choosing treatments and whether to refer to specialists; and controversial treatment possibilities such as arch expansion versus extraction for crowding, growth modification versus camouflage or surgery for skeletal problems, and the use of temporary anchorage devices (TADs). It also introduces a treatment planning sequence (Fig. 7.1) that moves from a prioritized problem list and goals through possible solutions and detailed planning to informed consent and execution.

nodes.title: Treatment Possibilities
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers key concepts in orthodontic treatment planning, emphasizing that treatment decisions should be based on patient-centered benefit, including cost-benefit and risk-benefit analyses, rather than merely technical feasibility. It highlights the importance of patient input and informed consent, the role of evidence-based predictability and complexity in treatment selection, and the distinctions between general practice and specialist care.

The text then discusses major treatment possibilities, particularly the extraction versus arch expansion debate for crowding, considering esthetics and stability, with guidelines for different levels of arch length discrepancy and dental protrusion. It addresses skeletal problems through orthodontic camouflage, orthognathic surgery, and growth modification, and introduces the growing role of temporary anchorage devices (TADs) with associated controversies.

The document also covers mini-esthetic and micro-esthetic considerations: improving the smile framework by addressing tooth display, gummy smile etiologies and treatments, transverse smile width, smile arc, and symmetry; and enhancing tooth appearance through reshaping, proportion changes such as canine substitution, managing black triangles, coordination with restorative dentists, and gingival contouring using lasers.

Finally, it outlines the steps in planning comprehensive orthodontic treatment, emphasizing the need to prioritize pathologic problems before developmental ones and to move systematically from a problem list through goals and possible solutions to a final plan.

nodes.title: Planning Comprehensive Orthodontic Treatment
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers key aspects of orthodontic treatment planning, including:

- Interaction between orthodontist and restorative dentist for small or discolored teeth, with two management approaches: post-orthodontic restorations using a retainer, or interim restorative work with bracket removal and replacement.
- Use of a soft tissue (diode) laser for reshaping gingival contours to improve tooth display, noting advantages over CO2 and Er:YAG lasers.

- Steps in planning comprehensive orthodontic treatment:
  - Distinguishing pathologic (disease-related) problems from developmental (orthodontic) problems; pathologic issues must be controlled first.
  - Prioritizing the orthodontic problem list, considering the patient's chief complaint, magnitude of problems, difficulty of treatment, and sequencing needs.
  - Setting treatment goals based on prioritized problems and patient attributes to maintain.
  - Evaluating treatment possibilities for each problem, considering growth modification, camouflage, surgery, and other options.
  - Analyzing interactions among possible solutions, potential compromises, and benefit versus cost/risk.
  - Considering special patient-specific factors before discussing options with the patient/parents.

- Development of the detailed treatment plan, specifying procedures and appliances while emphasizing that goals should determine mechanics, not vice versa.

- Informed consent: emphasizing patient comprehension, using teach-back/check-for-understanding, and discussing risks (pain, root resorption, white spot lesions, periodontal issues, trauma, retention).

- Common treatment risks and management: pain, root resorption, poor hygiene effects, white spot lesions, periodontal deterioration, and need for mouth guards during orthodontic treatment.

- Treatment planning in special circumstances: endodontically treated teeth, periodontal considerations (e.g., gingival grafts), and systemic diseases such as diabetes.

- The text uses a patient case (F.P.) throughout to illustrate the planning process, including problem lists, priorities, treatment goals, possible solutions, interactions, and final treatment plan.

nodes.title: Treatment Planning in Special Circumstances
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic treatment planning, emphasizing the interactive process between the doctor and patient in making final treatment decisions, including discussing alternatives such as headgear, extraction, or orthognathic surgery and obtaining informed consent. It then addresses treatment planning in special circumstances: dental disease problems (endodontically treated teeth, periodontal procedures), systemic disease problems (diabetes, arthritis, steroids/bisphosphonates, pregnancy), dental and jaw injuries (trauma, ankylosis, mandibular asymmetry, surgical intervention), and sleep apnea—focusing on pediatric OSA treatment with adenotonsillectomy and maxillary expansion, along with the dentist's role in screening and referral.

nodes.title: Treatment of OSA in Children
nodes.summary: The partial document covers several key areas in orthodontic treatment planning: considerations for medically complex patients (e.g., childhood cancer survivors) and the need for limited treatment scope in poor-prognosis cases; cautions and deferral of orthodontic treatment during pregnancy due to risks like gingival hyperplasia and bone turnover issues; management of dental and jaw injuries, including root resorption risks in traumatized teeth, repositioning of displaced maxilla, treatment of mandibular asymmetry based on condylar translation, and early surgical intervention for severe growth restriction; and a detailed section on sleep apnea, covering screening and referral, treatment options in children (adenotonsillectomy, maxillary expansion with limited evidence, mandibular advancement appliances, myofunctional therapy with adherence issues), and treatment in adults (effectiveness of oral appliances, comparison with CPAP, and dental side effects of both oral appliances and prolonged CPAP use).

nodes.title: Treatment of OSA in Adults
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic considerations in managing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in children and adults, and begins discussion of a craniofacial anomaly. It reviews pediatric OSA treatments including limited evidence for maxillary expansion, mandibular advancement appliances, and myofunctional therapy. For adults, it discusses the effectiveness and dental side effects of oral sleep appliances, maxillomandibular advancement surgery, soft tissue surgeries, and hypoglossal nerve stimulation. It also introduces hemimandibular hypertrophy, describing its cause, presentation, and surgical treatment options.

nodes.title: Common Dentofacial and Craniofacial Anomalies
nodes.summary: The partial document covers surgical management of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and common dentofacial/craniofacial anomalies. Key points include: maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) for OSA, with 85% of patients achieving >50% AHI reduction but less than 40% cure, and best outcomes in severe cases (AHI >60) with skeletal discrepancies; isolated mandibular setback for Class III is reconsidered due to potential airway effects, though average AHI showed no significant change in one study. Soft tissue surgeries (e.g., UPPP, tongue reduction) have variable success and rarely produce complete resolution. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is a newer treatment, requiring careful case selection (contraindicated in concentric palatal collapse and BMI >35).
