nodes.summary: The partial document covers growth modification techniques for Class II malocclusion, particularly focusing on vertical problems (deep bite and open bite) and facial asymmetry. It discusses headgear safety and proper use, then explains the interplay between vertical and anteroposterior skeletal problems. For short face/deep bite cases, it describes treatments like cervical headgear and functional appliances to increase posterior eruption and rotate the mandible downward. For long face/open bite cases, it outlines several approaches—high-pull headgear to molars or a maxillary splint, functional appliances with bite blocks, and combined headgear-functional appliance therapy—to control vertical maxillary growth and posterior eruption. Finally, it addresses facial asymmetry in children, mainly due to asymmetric mandibular deficiency from hemifacial microsomia or condylar fractures, and discusses diagnosis and growth modification strategies.

nodes.title: Facial Asymmetry in Children
nodes.summary: The partial document covers facial asymmetry in children, focusing on asymmetric mandibular deficiency and excess. It discusses the prevalence and causes of facial asymmetry, emphasizing mandibular involvement in most cases. It contrasts congenital hemifacial microsomia with acquired condylar fracture as causes of asymmetric mandibular deficiency, including differential diagnosis and the importance of mandibular translation for growth modification. Treatment with hybrid functional appliances is illustrated through a longitudinal case, and surgical intervention is noted only to enable growth in severe cases. It also introduces asymmetric mandibular excess (hemimandibular hyperplasia) as a progressive condition not amenable to growth modification, requiring surgical management.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document contains two main components: first, a list of references for Chapter 14 on growth modification in Class II, open bite/deep bite, and multidimensional problems; second, an introductory section on comprehensive orthodontic treatment in the early permanent dentition. The latter discusses the goals of comprehensive treatment, distinguishes it from mixed dentition/growth modification, notes that it typically requires fixed appliances or clear aligners, identifies adolescence as the ideal time, and acknowledges special considerations for adults. It also outlines the traditional three treatment stages (alignment and leveling, correction of molar relationship and space closure, finishing), explains how modern techniques have modified this framework (less extraction, variable sequencing, clear aligners), and previews the chapter contents for fixed appliance treatment with round wires, rectangular wires, finishing, and clear aligner therapy.

structure.title: Section 6: Comprehensive Orthodontic Treatment in the Early Permanent Dentition
structure.summary: The partial document introduces comprehensive orthodontic treatment in the early permanent dentition, emphasizing that it aims to achieve ideal occlusion by repositioning all or nearly all teeth, unlike mixed dentition or growth modification. It outlines the need for a second phase of comprehensive treatment after permanent teeth erupt, typically using fixed appliances or clear aligners, with ideal timing in adolescence and special considerations for adults. The text discusses Raymond Begg’s three stages of treatment (alignment and leveling, correction of molar relationship and space closure, and finishing) and how modern treatment differs, including less frequent extractions, variable sequencing, and the use of clear aligners. It then focuses on Chapter 15, which covers alignment and vertical problems in adolescents, including Class I crowding/protrusion, the importance of arch form, leveling by extrusion or intrusion, and the properties of alignment archwires. The chapter outline highlights correction of crowding, other space problems, and leveling techniques.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment in Adolescents: Alignment and Vertical Problems
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the beginning of a chapter on comprehensive treatment in adolescents, focusing on alignment and vertical problems. It introduces the chapter's scope: correcting crowding in patients with normal jaw relationships and addressing problems in all three planes of space caused by tooth displacement rather than jaw size discrepancies. Key points include the importance of alignment for all malocclusion patients, controlling incisor position, arch width and form, and leveling the curve of Spee. It stresses visualizing desired tooth positions before treatment, preserving the patient's original lower arch form for stability, and using appropriate archwires (e.g., superelastic A-NiTi) that reflect individual arch form. The section also begins discussing properties of alignment archwires, requiring strength, springiness, and a long range of action with a flat load-deflection curve delivering optimal tipping force.

nodes.title: Class I Crowding/Protrusion
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key concepts in orthodontic treatment for adolescents, focusing on alignment and vertical problems. It begins with an introduction to Class I crowding/protrusion, emphasizing the importance of alignment, arch form, and incisor position. The Alignment section discusses properties of alignment archwires, including superelastic nickel-titanium (A-NiTi) wires, force levels, and wire selection principles, as well as management of symmetric and asymmetric crowding, arch expansion techniques, and treatment of missing or malformed lateral incisors. Crossbite correction is addressed for both anterior and posterior dental crossbites, including methods like bite blocks, expansion arches, and cross-elastics. Other space problems include management of impacted or unerupted teeth (surgical exposure, attachment, mechanics), impacted lower second molars, and diastema closure with frenectomy considerations. Finally, the Leveling section discusses relative vs. absolute intrusion, with leveling by extrusion using exaggerated or reverse curves of Spee, and introduces leveling by intrusion.

nodes.title: Leveling
nodes.summary: The partial document focuses on orthodontic treatment of alignment and vertical problems in adolescents, specifically addressing methods for leveling the dental arch when an excessive curve of Spee is present. It contrasts relative intrusion (achieved by extrusion of posterior teeth) with absolute intrusion (true incisor intrusion). Key techniques discussed include leveling by extrusion using continuous archwires with exaggerated or reverse curves of Spee, archwire sequences (e.g., 16-mil steel, auxiliary leveling arches), and the pitfalls of rectangular wires with reverse curves causing undesired incisor root torque. Leveling by intrusion is described via three approaches: bypass archwires (e.g., 2×4 appliance, Ricketts' utility arch) with their limitations, segmented archwires (Burstone technique) using stabilized posterior segments, auxiliary intrusion arches, and precise force control, and aligners with attachments for relative intrusion. Additional topics include clear aligner therapy for overbite, management of impacted mandibular second molars (surgical uprighting, brass wire separators), treatment of maxillary midline diastema (frenectomy, bonded retainers), intrusion of maxillary posterior teeth using skeletal anchorage for open bite correction, and a case example of adult deep bite correction. The text also covers asymmetric intrusion, anchorage considerations, and preventing incisor tipping during intrusion.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document is from Chapter 16 of an orthodontic text, focusing on comprehensive treatment in adolescents, specifically space closure and Class II/III correction. It outlines topics such as sliding versus loop mechanics for space closure, correction of bimaxillary protrusion, maximum and minimum incisor retraction, Class II correction through differential growth or camouflage, and Class III camouflage. The text introduces the shift from alignment with round wires (Chapter 15) to bodily tooth movement and root torque with rectangular wires, and begins discussing incisor protrusion problems in bimaxillary protrusion, Class II, and Class III malocclusions, along with the pros and cons of sliding versus closing loop mechanics.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment in Adolescence: Space Closure and Class II/Class III Correction
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the beginning of Chapter 16 on comprehensive treatment in adolescence, focusing on space closure and Class II/III correction. It outlines the chapter topics, introduces three conditions with incisor protrusion (bimaxillary protrusion, Class II, and Class III malocclusion), and emphasizes camouflage treatment for acceptable dentofacial esthetics. It then discusses the two main methods for space closure: sliding mechanics and closing loop mechanics, comparing their advantages and disadvantages, including friction, root-paralleling moments, and mechanical complexity.

nodes.title: Space Closure in Incisor Protrusion Problems
nodes.summary: The partial document is from an orthodontics textbook chapter on comprehensive treatment in adolescence, focusing on space closure and correction of Class II/Class III malocclusion. It begins by outlining the chapter topics, then explains excessive incisor protrusion in three conditions: bimaxillary protrusion, Class II malocclusion, and Class III malocclusion. A major section compares sliding mechanics versus closing loop mechanics for space closure. For sliding mechanics, it covers the need for rectangular archwires, friction and binding, the automatic generation of root-paralleling moments, force sources like NiTi coil springs, and fail-safe characteristics. For closing loop mechanics, it discusses spring properties, wire material and size, root-paralleling moments with gable bends, loop location, and design principles such as fail-safe activation and the Opus loop. The document then details correction of bimaxillary protrusion, emphasizing moderate anchorage situations and space closure with both 22-slot and 18-slot edgewise appliances. It also covers maximum incisor retraction (maximum anchorage), including reinforcement with lingual arches, headgear, interarch elastics, two-step frictionless retraction, and skeletal anchorage. Minimum incisor retraction is addressed as well, focusing on closing spaces without retracting incisors, using anterior anchorage and skeletal anchorage. Finally, the text begins discussing Class II correction in adolescents, highlighting differential growth and the use of headgear and fixed functional appliances like the Herbst appliance for growth modification.

nodes.title: Class II Correction in Adolescents
nodes.summary: The partial document covers comprehensive orthodontic treatment in adolescents, focusing on Class II and Class III correction. It begins with Class II correction options: differential jaw growth via extraoral force or functional appliances, and differential tooth movement with or without extraction. It emphasizes that growth modification is most effective during the adolescent growth spurt, with timing differences between boys and girls. Headgear is discussed as a method for growth modification, including ideal patient selection, effects on maxillary teeth and space opening, and the importance of continuing headgear until the arch is consolidated. Fixed functional appliances, particularly the Herbst appliance, are described for early permanent dentition, with compatibility with fixed appliances. Class II camouflage is introduced for patients with reasonable jaw relationships, detailing three tooth-movement strategies: distal movement of upper molars, differential tooth movement using extraction spaces, and nonextraction treatment with lower arch forward movement. The document then thoroughly covers distal movement of upper molars, including limitations, molar rotation correction, and anchorage systems: headgear and Class II elastics (with drawbacks), skeletal anchorage via miniplates and palatal bone screws, and the need for second molar extraction in some cases. Differential anteroposterior tooth movement using extraction spaces is explained, including extraction of upper first premolars (with anchorage reinforcement), extraction of maxillary and mandibular premolars (e.g., upper first and lower second premolar extraction pattern), and nonextraction correction with interarch elastics, highlighting side effects like extrusion and occlusal plane rotation. Finally, Class III camouflage is briefly addressed, including retraction of lower incisors and use of Class III elastics, with caution about vertical effects.

nodes.title: Class III Camouflage
nodes.summary: The partial document covers aspects of orthodontic treatment in adolescence, focusing on space closure and Class II/Class III correction. It discusses hemisection for space closure, the use and effects of interarch elastics for nonextraction Class II correction (including force magnitudes, anchorage considerations, and vertical/rotational side effects), and the limitations of prolonged heavy elastic wear. It also addresses Class III camouflage strategies, including the use of Class III elastics, extraction patterns (e.g., lower incisor extraction, premolar extractions), and skeletal anchorage for mandibular arch distalization, with attention to patient-specific factors such as growth, facial esthetics, and ethnic differences. The text includes clinical examples and figures, and ends with a reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document focuses on two main aspects of orthodontic treatment. First, it briefly discusses treatment options for late adolescent Class III patients, including extraction of second premolars to minimize incisor changes and the use of skeletal anchorage to move the lower arch posteriorly, often requiring third molar extraction. Second, it introduces a chapter on "Comprehensive Treatment: Finishing," outlining the final stage of orthodontic treatment. This includes correcting individual tooth positions, midline discrepancies, tooth size discrepancies, root paralleling, torque, vertical incisor relationships (overbite and open bite), and final settling of teeth. It also covers special finishing procedures to avoid relapse, micro-esthetic procedures, and a logical archwire sequence for edgewise technique, emphasizing the need for proper bracket positioning and the use of appropriately flexible finishing wires.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment: Finishing
nodes.summary: The partial document is from a chapter on "Comprehensive Treatment: Finishing" in orthodontics. It outlines the key topics covered in the chapter, including adjustment of individual tooth positions, midline and tooth size discrepancies, root paralleling, torque, correction of vertical incisor relationships (excessive overbite and anterior open bite), final settling of teeth, methods for settling, control of rebound and posturing, removal of bands, use of positioners and aligners, special procedures to avoid relapse, control of unfavorable growth, and micro-esthetic procedures such as gingival recontouring and tooth reshaping. The introductory text explains that the finishing stage focuses on perfecting details after major alignment and occlusion are achieved. It discusses differences between the Begg technique and contemporary edgewise techniques, the importance of appropriate archwire sequences and sizes to fill the bracket slot, and specifics on adjusting individual tooth positions, including when to rebond brackets versus using compensating bends.

nodes.title: Adjustment of Individual Tooth Positions
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the finishing stage of comprehensive orthodontic treatment, focusing on obtaining precise dental alignment and occlusion details after major tooth movements are completed. Key points include: (1) adjustment of individual tooth positions, including bracket rebonding, step bends in flexible full-dimension wires, and managing in-out/up-down discrepancies; (2) correction of midline discrepancies through asymmetric Class II/III elastics, archwire steps, and addressing transverse arch relationships or skeletal asymmetries; (3) management of tooth-size discrepancies using interproximal enamel reduction, composite build-ups for small maxillary lateral incisors, and compensation via incisor torque adjustments; (4) root paralleling techniques, including the use of resilient rectangular archwires (beta-Ti and M-NiTi), panoramic radiographs to assess root position, and tie-back mechanics to prevent spaces from opening; (5) torque application—lingual root torque of incisors via archwires or auxiliaries such as the Burstone torquing arch, factors controlling torque expression (wire size, bracket slot play, torsion), and buccal root torque of maxillary premolars/canines for improved smile esthetics; and (6) the beginning of correction of vertical incisor relationships, addressing excessive overbite with careful assessment of maxillary incisor display and anterior face height. The text also contrasts classic Begg (and Tip-Edge) techniques with contemporary edgewise appliances and discusses archwire sequencing principles using 17 × 25 and 21 × 25 wires.

nodes.title: Correction of Vertical Incisor Relationships
nodes.summary: The partial document covers finishing techniques in orthodontic treatment, focusing on torque control and vertical correction. Key points include: effective torque expression using rectangular archwires (especially for Class II division 2 with lingually tipped incisors), factors affecting torque (wire stiffness, slot inclination, and wire-bracket fit), and recommendations for finishing wires in 22-slot appliances (e.g., 21 × 25 beta-Ti). It also discusses buccal root torque of maxillary premolars and canines for improved smile esthetics, and correction of vertical incisor relationships, addressing excessive overbite (via intrusion or posterior elongation) and anterior open bite (via posterior intrusion with skeletal anchorage or lower incisor elongation). Finally, it describes methods for final settling of teeth into occlusion, including replacing rectangular archwires with light round wires, using vertical elastics, or employing tooth positioners/aligners.

nodes.title: Final “Settling” of Teeth
nodes.summary: The partial document covers final finishing procedures in orthodontic treatment. It discusses using vertical elastics to close open bites or deepen bites with flexible archwires, noting stability considerations for incisor elongation. It describes the need for final "settling" of teeth into occlusion after rectangular archwires, and presents three settling methods: light round archwires with vertical elastics, laced posterior elastics after removing posterior wire segments, and tooth positioners or aligners. It also addresses control of rebound and posturing after Class II/III correction, with guidelines for overcorrection and elastic weaning. The removal of bands and bonded brackets is detailed, including techniques for debonding metal and ceramic brackets, risks of enamel damage (with data from a study), management of residual resin, and the use of positioners or clear aligners for final finishing after appliance removal.

nodes.title: Positioners and Aligners for Finishing
nodes.summary: The partial document covers three main areas: (1) debonding of ceramic brackets, including three approaches to facilitate removal (modifying the bracket-resin interface, using heat, and engineering brackets to fracture predictably), plus techniques for cleaning residual resin and ceramic fragments from teeth; (2) the use of tooth positioners and limited series of clear aligners for finishing and final settling, including indications, fabrication steps, advantages (earlier appliance removal, reduced gingival inflammation) and disadvantages (cost, overbite increase, patient cooperation); and (3) special finishing procedures to avoid relapse, focusing on controlling unfavorable growth through active retention (headgear or modified functional appliances) and controlling tissue rebound through overtreatment and adjunctive periodontal surgery, with specific overtreatment recommendations for Class II/III correction, crossbite, crowding, and rotations.

nodes.title: Special Finishing Procedures to Avoid Relapse
nodes.summary: The partial document covers finishing procedures in comprehensive orthodontic treatment, focusing on final tooth settling and relapse prevention. It describes the use of tooth positioners or aligners for final settling, including fabrication steps, advantages (earlier appliance removal, reduced gingival inflammation) and disadvantages (cost, increased overbite, poor rotation control, need for cooperation). It then addresses special finishing procedures to avoid relapse, distinguishing between continued unfavorable growth and tissue rebound. For growth control, active retention with extraoral force or modified functional appliances is discussed. For rebound control, overtreatment strategies for Class II/III, crossbite, crowding, and rotations are outlined, along with adjunctive periodontal surgery such as circumferential supracrestal fibrotomy (CSF) and the papilla-dividing procedure to section elastic gingival fibers, with indications for rotated teeth and timing considerations. Finally, the document touches on micro-esthetic procedures, specifically gingival recontouring to improve tooth proportions and display before enamel recontouring.

nodes.title: Micro-Esthetic Procedures in Finishing
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers two main topics in orthodontic finishing: adjunctive periodontal surgery to prevent relapse and micro-esthetic procedures to enhance smile appearance.

1. **Sectioning Elastic Gingival Fibers**: Discusses the role of stretched supracrestal gingival fibers in orthodontic relapse, especially for rotated teeth. Describes surgical techniques to cut these fibers, including circumferential supracrestal fibrotomy (CSF) using a blade or laser, and an alternative papilla-dividing (papilla split) procedure. Highlights timing (after alignment and retention), indications (severely rotated teeth, not simple crowding), and equivalence of methods in improving stability.

2. **Micro-Esthetic Procedures in Finishing**: Focuses on soft tissue and enamel recontouring to improve tooth proportions and display. Key points include:
   - Addressing gingival overgrowth first (e.g., laser gingivectomy) to correct crown height-width ratios.
   - Reshaping teeth (enameloplasty) after alignment to refine height-width ratios, connector lengths, and embrasure forms.
   - A detailed case example (Figs. 17.20–17.22) illustrating micro-esthetic diagnosis and treatment: correcting central incisor height, narrowing wide centrals, closing black triangles, and refining incisal embrasures.
   - Collaboration with restorative dentistry for malformed or damaged teeth, using temporary laminates and final veneers to achieve optimal results.

The text also includes references and emphasizes that these finishing details are simple yet highly valued by patients.

nodes.title: Clear Aligners in Adolescents
nodes.summary: The partial document provides a chapter outline for a text on clear aligners in adolescents, followed by an introductory section on the development of aligner treatment. Main points covered include: the chapter's listed topics (ranging from aligner versus fixed appliances, benefits/limitations, treatment goals, management of various corrections, hybrid treatment, impacted teeth, space closure, finishing, and success strategies); the historical evolution of clear aligners enabled by digital software and 3D printing, with Align Technology's Invisalign receiving FDA clearance in 1998; current estimates that over 30% of U.S. orthodontic cases use aligners; a description of aligners as digitally designed plastic trays that move teeth in stages; the displacement-driven nature of treatment and the shift toward force-driven planning; common wear schedules (typically 7-day changes, sometimes 10-14 days); monitoring and refinement via scans; differences from fixed appliances in making adjustments; and the strategy of prioritizing challenging movements in initial attachment design and staging.

nodes.title: Development of Aligner Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers an overview of clear aligner treatment in adolescents from a dental textbook. It includes a chapter outline and discusses the development of aligner therapy, comparing aligners to fixed appliances. Key topics include the benefits and limitations of aligners (esthetics, oral hygiene, no food restrictions; potential decalcification risks and attachment visibility), treatment goals and virtual setup (digital planning, simulating final occlusion, handling eruption), and management differences with aligners (fewer emergencies, longer visit intervals, remote monitoring, compliance challenges, and costs). The document also begins detailing tooth alignment concepts, focusing on simple spacing—covering biomechanics, attachment design for tipping and root movement, staging of space closure, and methods like overcorrection aligners to ensure complete contact closure.

nodes.title: Tooth Alignment Concepts
nodes.summary: The partial document covers principles and considerations for tooth alignment using clear aligner therapy in the early permanent dentition. It begins with intra-arch movements such as rotations, leveling, spacing, and crowding, emphasizing biomechanics, attachment design, and staging. Specific topics include: simple spacing closure, the role of attachments for tipping, extrusion/intrusion control, and bodily movement; staging and planning strategies for space closure, including overcorrection aligners and leaf gauge measurement; management of mild crowding, addressing space creation, rotations, and attachment needs; complex crowding, including adjunctive methods like buttons and elastics; and an introduction to overall arch alignment in anteroposterior, vertical, and transverse dimensions. Clinical examples and figures illustrate attachment designs, force application principles, and treatment outcomes.

nodes.title: Management of A–P, Vertical, and Transverse Correction
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the use of clear aligners in adolescents, focusing on complex crowding and three-dimensional correction. It discusses the importance of attachment design and interproximal reduction (IPR) for managing significant crowding, as well as adjunctive aids like bonded buttons and elastic chains to improve rotational forces. It emphasizes that planned digital movements are not fully realized clinically—only about 50% of movements are achieved—requiring overcorrection and refinements. The section on A–P, vertical, and transverse correction details methods for Class II correction using elastics, functional appliances (e.g., MARA, Twin Block, Invisalign MA), and extractions; Class III correction via reversed elastics, IPR, and potential camouflage or surgery; openbite correction through anterior extrusion/posterior intrusion with overcorrection; deep bite correction using posterior attachments, bite ramps, and significant overcorrection; and transverse correction with fixed expanders (RPE/MARPE), aligner-only expansion, or cross elastics. Finally, it introduces hybrid treatment for impacted or ectopic teeth and other complex cases where aligners alone are insufficient.

nodes.title: Hybrid Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key considerations for clear aligner treatment in adolescents, focusing on transverse correction, hybrid techniques, and strategies for successful treatment. It discusses methods for transverse correction including fixed expanders (RPE, MARPE), aligner-only expansion, and cross elastics, emphasizing the need for overcorrection. Hybrid treatment is described for cases requiring additional techniques, such as managing impacted or ectopic teeth using elastics or temporary anchorage devices (TADs), complex space closure or root uprighting with limited fixed appliances, and finishing cases originally started with fixed appliances. The final section on strategies for success addresses digital setups and staging principles, including overcorrection recommendations for various tooth movements, staging movements for predictable tracking, and attachment design considerations for effective aligner force delivery and retention.

nodes.title: Strategies for Success
nodes.summary: The partial document covers strategies for successful clear aligner treatment in adolescents, emphasizing proper treatment goals, digital setup and staging principles (including overcorrection, staging movements, and prioritizing movements in complex cases), attachment design considerations (optimized attachments, retention, and avoiding overuse), and case monitoring/compliance (aligner tracking, virtual monitoring, and adjustments like IPR or plier dimpling). It also includes a table of recommended overcorrections for tooth movements and references.

It then transitions to the beginning of Chapter 19 on retention, presenting a chapter outline that includes the necessity of retention, periodontal tissue reorganization, growth-related changes, types of retainers (removable, fixed, active), and specific clinical applications. The text begins explaining why retention is necessary, citing factors like unstable tooth positions, soft tissue pressures, and continued growth, and starts detailing the reorganization of the periodontal ligament and gingival tissues after orthodontic treatment.

nodes.title: Retention
nodes.summary: The partial document is from an orthodontic textbook chapter on retention. It begins with a chapter outline listing topics such as the necessity of retention, tissue reorganization, growth-related occlusal changes, timing of retention, various retainer types, and space maintenance. The text then introduces the importance of retention, emphasizing that treatment is not complete when appliances are removed and that retention planning must be part of the original treatment plan. The first major section, "Why Is Retention Necessary?", explains that most orthodontic results are potentially unstable and retention is needed for three reasons: periodontal/gingival tissue reorganization, unstable tooth positions leading to relapse from soft tissue pressures, and continued growth altering results. It also notes that retention is essential until growth is complete, and permanent retention may be required for unstable positions. The second section, "Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues," describes how orthodontic tooth movement widens the periodontal ligament and disrupts collagen fibers, requiring time for recovery. It states that passive archwires do not count as retention, and once teeth can respond individually to chewing forces, PDL reorganization occurs over 3-4 months. This reorganization is vital for stability because the periodontal system contributes to the equilibrium controlling tooth position, resisting small prolonged imbalances in soft tissue pressures.

nodes.title: Why Is Retention Necessary?
nodes.summary: The partial document is from an orthodontics textbook chapter on "Retention," and it begins with a chapter outline listing topics such as the necessity of retention, tissue reorganization, growth-related occlusal changes, timing of retention, and various retainer types. The main content explains that retention is critical because orthodontic results are potentially unstable. It identifies three major reasons for retention: gingival and periodontal tissues need time to reorganize after tooth movement, teeth may be in inherently unstable positions, and continued growth can alter results. The section on periodontal and gingival tissue reorganization discusses the widening of the periodontal ligament, disruption of collagen fibers, the role of active stabilization, and the slower remodeling of gingival fibers, leading to principles such as daily wear for the first 3–4 months and at least 12 months of retention. The document then covers occlusal changes related to growth, detailing how class II, class III, deep bite, and open bite patterns can relapse due to differential jaw growth and offering specific retention strategies for each, including the use of functional appliances, bite plates, and control of posterior tooth eruption. It also emphasizes the need to retain lower incisor alignment until mandibular growth declines. A summary of retention timing states that daily wear is needed initially, followed by part-time wear for at least 12 months, and continued until growth is complete. Finally, the partial document introduces removable retainers, focusing on Hawley retainers, including their design, clasps, modifications for extraction spaces, and the importance of an acrylic bite plane for overbite control.

nodes.title: Removable Retainers
nodes.summary:
The partial document focuses on orthodontic retention, emphasizing the need and timing for retention, types of retainers, and key clinical considerations.

Main points covered:

- **Retention of lower incisor alignment**: Continued mandibular growth can cause lower incisor crowding by tipping incisors lingually, so retention is needed until growth declines. Late third-molar pressure is not considered a cause of late crowding, but prolonged retention until the late teens/early 20s is reasonable. Adults often show some late lower incisor crowding, and fixed lingual retainers reduce this significantly. Prediction of who will relapse is difficult, so patient-specific decisions are recommended; a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to favor one retention approach.

- **Timing of retention**: All patients treated with fixed appliances or aligners need retention: full-time or daily wear for the first 3–4 months, then part-time wear for at least 12 months, and continuing part-time if significant growth remains.

- **Removable retainers**:
  - **Hawley retainers**: Traditional maxillary retainers with molar clasps and a labial bow; they can control overbite, allow posterior settling when acrylic is trimmed, and can be modified for extraction cases to keep spaces closed. Clasp placement and acrylic height are important design considerations.
  - **Spring/clip retainers**: Plastic bars on labial and lingual tooth surfaces, useful for preventing spaces from reopening; the Moore retainer is a mandibular extension used in extraction cases.
  - **Clear/vacuum-formed retainers**: Popular and esthetic, with good patient compliance and effectiveness for maintaining incisor alignment. Limitations include possible posterior open bite, less bite-depth control, less transverse rigidity, and wear over time. Final aligners are less effective as retainers than more rigid materials.
  - **Positioners**: Can serve as retainers and have the advantage of maintaining occlusal relationships; they are useful in open-bite and unfavorable-growth cases.

- **Fixed retainers**: Bonded retainers are used for long-term stabilization, especially for maintaining lower incisor position during late growth, holding diastemas closed, and maintaining posterior tooth position in adults. A bonded canine-to-canine lingual bar can effectively preserve lower incisor alignment without harming periodontal health over the long term.

nodes.title: Fixed Retainers
nodes.summary: The partial document covers two main topics in retention: fixed retainers and active retainers. For fixed retainers, it describes their indications, including maintaining lower incisor position during late growth, maintaining diastema closure, and maintaining space for future implants or bridges. It discusses specific designs such as canine-to-canine bonded lingual bars and flexible wires bonded to incisors, along with wire sizes and bonding considerations. It also highlights risks of inadvertent tooth movement from fixed lingual retainers, even when passive, and emphasizes the need for long-term professional supervision. For active retainers, it explains their use in realigning irregular incisors, often after interproximal reduction, using spring retainers or 3D-printed aligners, and describes modified functional appliances for correcting mild occlusal relapse tendencies such as Class II or Class III discrepancies.

nodes.title: Active Retainers
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses active retainers in orthodontic retention. It defines active retainers as devices that both move teeth and retain them, typically used for relapse or growth changes. Main points include: realignment of irregular lower incisors using interproximal reduction (IPR) followed by active canine-to-canine spring retainers or 3D-printed aligners; the procedure for fabricating such retainers; consideration of fixed appliances for more severe relapse; and the use of modified functional appliances (activators or Bionators) as active retainers to correct up to 3 mm of class II or class III occlusal relapse, mainly in growing teenagers. It also includes figures illustrating Hawley retainers with pontics, interproximal enamel removal, clip-on active retainers, and fixed appliance retreatment.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document begins with a list of references for Chapter 19 on retention, followed by the opening of a section on treatment for adults. It highlights the rapid growth of adult orthodontics and explains key differences from adolescent treatment, including the frequent need for interdisciplinary dental care, increased periodontal considerations, and the absence of growth, which eliminates growth modification as an option. It outlines important treatment planning principles for adults: involving all relevant dentists, starting with the final result in mind, setting realistic rather than ideal goals, addressing adults' psychological responses and pain tolerance, and ensuring disease control before orthodontic treatment. It then previews upcoming chapters: Chapter 20 on interactions with other dental specialists, Chapter 21 on clear aligners for adults, and Chapter 22 on orthognathic surgery. Finally, the document introduces Chapter 20, "Special Considerations in Treatment for Adults," defining the difference between adjunctive and comprehensive treatment, describing the two main adult patient groups (younger adults seeking comprehensive care and older adults needing orthodontics as part of larger restorative/periodontal treatment), and noting that comprehensive adult treatment is technically demanding with options limited to camouflage, skeletal anchorage, or surgery.

structure.title: Special Considerations in Treatment for Adults
structure.summary: The partial document introduces a chapter on special considerations in orthodontic treatment for adults. It begins with a chapter outline listing key topics such as adjunctive versus comprehensive treatment, treatment goals, biomechanics, adjunctive procedures, comprehensive treatment considerations, and more. The main content covered defines adults by growth completion (age cutoffs around 18 for females, 20-21 for males) and identifies two adult patient groups: younger adults seeking comprehensive orthodontic treatment for quality-of-life improvement, and older adults needing orthodontics as part of a larger plan to maintain dental health. It distinguishes adjunctive orthodontic treatment (simpler, focused tooth movement to facilitate other dental procedures) from comprehensive treatment, and briefly discusses principles of adjunctive treatment, including goals, diagnosis, biomechanics, and timing.

nodes.title: Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document focuses on special considerations in orthodontic treatment for adults. It begins by defining adults as patients whose growth is essentially complete, with age cutoffs around 18 for females and 20-21 for males. It distinguishes two groups of adult patients: younger adults seeking comprehensive treatment for quality-of-life improvement, and older adults needing orthodontics as an adjunct to broader periodontal and restorative care. The text contrasts adjunctive versus comprehensive treatment in terms of goals, scope, duration, and complexity. It outlines the principles of adjunctive treatment, including treatment goals such as improving periodontal health, establishing favorable crown-to-root ratios, and facilitating restorative procedures. It also lists common adjunctive procedures (e.g., uprighting posterior teeth, crossbite correction, extrusion, aligning anterior teeth) and important corollaries, such as TMD treatment not being adjunctive and limitations on enamel stripping. Finally, it discusses diagnostic and treatment planning considerations for adjunctive treatment, emphasizing the need for an adequate diagnostic database, appropriate radiographs, articulator-mounted casts, realistic treatment planning, and efficient tooth movement within about six months.

nodes.title: Principles of Adjunctive Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key aspects of orthodontic treatment for adults, focusing on the distinction between adjunctive and comprehensive orthodontics. It outlines the goals of adjunctive treatment, which include improving periodontal health, establishing favorable crown-to-root ratios, and facilitating restorative procedures. Common adjunctive procedures are described, such as repositioning teeth for implants or prostheses, aligning anterior teeth for esthetics, correcting crossbites, and forced eruption of broken-down teeth. Important limitations and corollaries are noted, including that TMD treatment is not adjunctive, intrusion is best managed by orthodontists, and enamel stripping is limited for minor crowding. Diagnostic and treatment planning considerations emphasize the need for a complete problem list, appropriate radiographs, and realistic rather than ideal treatment goals, with adjunctive treatment typically completed within six months. Biomechanical considerations address appliance selection—favoring fixed edgewise appliances or clear aligners for anterior alignment—and the effects of reduced periodontal support, requiring lighter forces and larger moments. The timing and sequence of treatment are also covered, stressing control of active dental disease and periodontal health before orthodontic movement. Finally, the section begins discussing specific adjunctive procedures, particularly uprighting posterior teeth, including treatment planning considerations such as whether to upright third molars and whether to move crowns distally or roots mesially.

nodes.title: Adjunctive Treatment Procedures
nodes.summary: The partial document covers adjunctive orthodontic procedures for adults, including molar uprighting (treatment planning, appliances for distal crown tipping and mesial root movement, final positioning, uprighting two molars, and retention), crossbite correction, tooth extrusion (controlled extrusion and conventional orthodontic extrusion), alignment of anterior teeth (diastema closure, space redistribution, and management of crowded/rotated/displaced incisors), obstructive sleep apnea-related orthodontic procedures (effectiveness and dental side effects of oral appliances and CPAP), and comprehensive treatment in adults with psychologic considerations.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment in Adults
nodes.summary: The partial document covers special considerations in adult orthodontic treatment, including methods for aligning mildly irregular lower incisors via enamel stripping or lower incisor extraction, with caution about potential adverse effects and the need for diagnostic setup. It emphasizes retention strategies after tooth movement, such as thermoplastic retainers or bonded fixed retainers. It then discusses obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)-related orthodontic procedures, detailing the effectiveness and limitations of oral appliance therapy compared to CPAP, including mean disease alleviation. It highlights dental side effects of mandibular advancing appliances, such as reduced overjet/overbite, anterior crossbites, and tooth movement over time, as well as dental changes from prolonged CPAP use. It stresses informed consent and considerations before orthodontic treatment in OSA patients. Finally, it introduces psychologic considerations in comprehensive adult treatment, contrasting adult motivation with the passive acceptance typical of younger patients.

nodes.title: Special Considerations in Treatment for Adults

It then discusses obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) treatment, focusing on the effectiveness and limitations of oral appliances vs. CPAP, dental side effects such as tooth movement and occlusal changes from long-term use, and important pre-orthodontic considerations for OSA patients.
