key_items: Dental Side Effects of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers several adult orthodontic treatment topics. It discusses methods for managing lower incisor crowding, including enamel stripping and clear aligner therapy, as well as extraction of a lower incisor for severe crowding, noting the need for caution and diagnostic setups. It also addresses retention strategies after alignment. The text then covers obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)-related orthodontic procedures, explaining the effectiveness and limitations of oral appliance therapy compared to CPAP, and detailing dental side effects such as tooth movement, occlusal changes (reduced overjet/overbite, anterior crossbites), and spacing from prolonged CPAP use. Finally, it introduces comprehensive treatment in adults, beginning with psychologic considerations and how adult motivation for orthodontic treatment differs from that of younger patients.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment in Adults
nodes.summary: The partial document covers several key topics: methods for aligning adult teeth (using NiTi wires, enamel stripping, and lower incisor extraction), with cautions about side effects and the need for diagnostic setups; treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) via oral appliances, including their effectiveness compared to CPAP and the concept of mean disease alleviation; dental side effects of OSA treatments (tooth movement from mandibular advancing appliances and CPAP use, with long-term occlusal changes and informed consent considerations); and psychological considerations in comprehensive adult orthodontic treatment.

nodes.title: Psychologic Considerations
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers several key topics in adult orthodontic treatment. It begins with techniques for aligning crowded teeth, including the use of NiTi wires, enamel stripping for mild crowding, and lower incisor extraction for severe cases, with cautions about side effects and the need for diagnostic setups. It also addresses retention and relapse prevention, such as fiberotomy and various retainer options.

The text then discusses obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)-related orthodontic procedures, focusing on the effectiveness of mandibular advancing oral appliances, their variable success rates, and the concept of mean disease alleviation compared to CPAP. It details the dental side effects of OSA treatments, including tooth movement, occlusal changes (reduced overjet/overbite, anterior crossbites), and spacing from CPAP use, emphasizing informed consent and considerations for orthodontic correction in these patients.

Next, it covers comprehensive treatment in adults, particularly psychologic considerations. It contrasts adult motivations with those of adolescents, highlights the importance of realistic expectations and hidden agendas, and discusses aesthetic appliance options (ceramic brackets, lingual appliances, clear aligners) and their compromises. The text also addresses management of adult patients, including their need for explanation, potential compliance issues, and the benefits of treating adults.

Finally, the document examines temporomandibular dysfunction (TMD) as a reason for orthodontic treatment. It distinguishes between muscle-related and joint-related TMD, notes the controversial relationship between occlusion and TMD, and explains conditions like disc displacement and myofascial pain. It advises caution in using orthodontics to treat TMD, suggesting simpler methods like splints may be more appropriate.

nodes.title: Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers temporomandibular dysfunction (TMD) as a reason for orthodontic treatment in adults. It discusses the controversial relationship between occlusion and TMD, classification of TMD into muscle disorders, joint disorders, hypomobility, and growth disorders, with emphasis on distinguishing muscle vs. joint problems. It addresses arthritic changes, disc displacement, and myofascial pain from clenching/grinding, including their diagnosis and imaging. Treatment indications are outlined: stress reduction, behavioral adaptation, and occlusal modification via orthodontics or surgery only after conservative methods fail. The text also explains why orthodontic treatment may temporarily relieve symptoms, the risk of recurrence after treatment, complications from prior splint therapy (e.g., posterior open bite), and methods to manage these issues. Additionally, it briefly introduces periodontal considerations relevant to adult orthodontic treatment.

nodes.title: Periodontal Considerations
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic treatment considerations for adults, focusing on TMD-related issues and periodontal health. Key points include the need to avoid prolonged use of Class II or III elastics, especially in adults with TMD; the risk of symptom recurrence after orthodontic treatment, often requiring interocclusal splints; and complications from prior splint therapy, such as posterior open bite from anterior tooth eruption, managed by extruding posterior teeth with light vertical elastics. The document also emphasizes the growing importance of periodontal evaluation in adult patients, noting age-related prevalence of periodontal pockets and mucogingival problems, the episodic nature of periodontal disease, and the need to control periodontal disease before orthodontic treatment. It discusses management of minimal periodontal involvement, including risks of gingival recession from labial tooth movement and the value of gingival grafts, as well as treatment for moderate periodontal involvement, which requires preliminary periodontal therapy, observation, and deferral of surgical maintenance procedures until final occlusion is established.

nodes.title: Treatment of Patients With Minimal Periodontal Involvement
nodes.summary: The partial document covers periodontal considerations for adult orthodontic patients. It discusses the age-related prevalence of periodontal disease and mucogingival problems, the episodic nature of periodontal disease, and methods for identifying high-risk patients, including bleeding on probing and newer diagnostic tests. It describes three risk groups for periodontal bone loss progression and emphasizes that controlled periodontal disease does not contraindicate adult orthodontic treatment. For patients with minimal periodontal involvement, it stresses oral hygiene, the risk of gingival recession during tooth movement, the importance of attached gingival width and thickness, and the value of preventive gingival grafts. For patients with moderate periodontal involvement, it recommends controlling disease first, removing irritants, deferring maintenance procedures until after orthodontics, and allowing a healing/observation period before comprehensive treatment. A figure illustrating the prevalence of pocketing and inadequate attached gingiva by age is also referenced.

nodes.title: Moderate Periodontal Involvement
nodes.summary: The partial document covers periodontal considerations in adult orthodontic treatment. It discusses the age-related prevalence of periodontal pockets and inadequate attached gingiva, the episodic nature of periodontal disease, and risk groups for bone loss. It emphasizes controlling active periodontal disease before orthodontic treatment, and outlines management strategies for patients with minimal, moderate, and severe periodontal involvement—including oral hygiene, gingival grafting to prevent recession, preliminary periodontal therapy, maintenance schedules, and modified orthodontic mechanics. It also includes clinical examples and figures illustrating treatment approaches for periodontally compromised adults.

nodes.title: Severe Periodontal Involvement
nodes.summary: The partial document covers special considerations in orthodontic treatment for adults with periodontal and prosthodontic issues. For moderate periodontal involvement, it emphasizes regular periodontal maintenance at 2–4 month intervals, use of non-elastomeric ligation to reduce plaque, and adjunctive chemical agents such as chlorhexidine. For severe periodontal involvement, modifications include more frequent periodontal maintenance (every 4–6 weeks) and minimizing orthodontic forces to account for reduced periodontal ligament area and altered center of resistance; figures illustrate appropriate force/moment systems and gingival grafting before tooth movement. It also discusses the importance of crown-root ratio, selective crown reduction of lower incisors, cautious management of upper incisors, and the possibility of orthodontic treatment without further bone loss when periodontal health is controlled, though improvement is not guaranteed. The text then addresses prosthodontic-implant interactions, including positioning worn, damaged, or abraded teeth with the final restoration in mind. Key considerations are total space creation, mesiodistal positioning, buccolingual placement, and vertical positioning, along with early consultation with the restorative dentist and restoration-specific decisions such as crowns versus veneers.

nodes.title: Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic considerations for adult patients with periodontal bone loss, emphasizing reduced periodontal ligament area and altered force/moment requirements, the importance of crown-root ratio, and treatment strategies like crown shortening versus intrusion. It also discusses prosthodontic-implant interactions, including planning tooth position for restorations in cases of tooth structure loss, with attention to mesiodistal, buccolingual, and vertical positioning. A figure illustrates how bone loss affects force and moment needed for tooth movement.

nodes.title: Problems Related to Loss of Tooth Structure
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic considerations in adult patients with periodontal disease, including adjusting force and moment for teeth with reduced bone support, crown-root ratio and treatment of elongated incisors, and the potential for orthodontic treatment without worsening periodontal conditions. It also addresses prosthodontic-implant interactions: positioning worn or damaged teeth for restorations (space, mesiodistal, buccolingual, and vertical considerations), managing gingival esthetic problems (excessive gingival display and black triangles from recession), and treatment planning for missing teeth—including difficulties with closing old extraction sites, space closure after tooth loss due to periodontal disease (with special consideration of aggressive periodontitis), and integrating orthodontics with future implant placement and bone grafting.

nodes.title: Gingival Esthetic Problems
nodes.summary: The partial document covers several key topics in adult orthodontic treatment: gingival esthetic problems, including uneven gingival margins and black triangles from recession; considerations for tooth elongation vs. intrusion; challenges of closing old extraction sites due to alveolar bone remodeling; management of missing first molars and teeth lost to periodontal disease, including aggressive juvenile periodontitis; and orthodontic treatment planning for patients who will receive implants.

nodes.title: Missing Teeth: Space Closure Versus Prosthetic Replacement
key_items: Tooth Loss Due to Periodontal Disease
Comprehensive Orthodontics in Patients in Whom Implants Are Planned
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key adult orthodontic treatment considerations, including gingival esthetic issues (uneven margins, gummy smile, black triangles), challenges of closing old extraction sites due to alveolar bone remodeling, space closure versus prosthetic replacement for missing teeth, management of tooth loss from periodontal disease (including aggressive juvenile periodontitis), timing and coordination of orthodontics with implants and bone grafts, management of ankylosed teeth in implant planning, and advances in lingual orthodontics using custom brackets and wire-bending robots.

nodes.title: Complex Treatment Procedures
key_items: Clear Aligner Therapy in Complex Cases
nodes.summary: The partial document covers special considerations in adult orthodontic treatment, focusing on implant timing issues, lingual orthodontics, clear aligner therapy, and skeletal anchorage. Key points include: the risks of placing implants too early due to continued vertical growth, which can cause relative intrusion and esthetic problems; advances in lingual orthodontics using custom brackets and robotic wire bending for precise tooth movement; clinical cases illustrating management of missing teeth, ankylosed incisors, and space closure with lingual appliances; a brief introduction to clear aligner therapy for complex cases; and the beginning of a section on four major applications of skeletal anchorage in adults.

nodes.title: Applications of Skeletal Anchorage
nodes.summary: The partial document covers aspects of adult orthodontic treatment, including clear aligner therapy for complex cases and skeletal anchorage applications. It notes that complex clear aligner treatment requires modified sequencing, reduced tooth movements, and frequent revision aligners. Skeletal anchorage has four major applications: positioning individual teeth, retracting protruding incisors, moving molars distally or mesially, and intruding teeth to correct open or deep bites. The text focuses in detail on retraction of protruding incisors using skeletal anchorage, including palatal implants, bone screws, miniplates, and managing bimaxillary protrusion, with discussion of bony spicules caused by differential alveolar bone remodeling.

nodes.title: Retraction of Protruding Incisors
nodes.summary: The partial document covers advanced adult orthodontic treatment techniques, focusing on skeletal anchorage for retraction of protruding incisors and distal movement of dental arches. It discusses retraction of maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth using bone screws and palatal implants, as well as whole-arch distalization with miniplates or buccal shelf screws. It also explains the occurrence of bony spicules after incisor retraction in some Asian adults as differential alveolar bone remodeling rather than exostoses. Additional topics include combined retraction and intrusion of protrusive incisors using segmented arch mechanics, and a case example of mandibular arch distalization with bone screws to correct crossbite in an Asian adult.

nodes.title: Retraction and Intrusion of Protruding Incisors
nodes.summary: The partial document covers orthodontic treatment considerations for adults, focusing on managing protrusion and malocclusion with skeletal anchorage. Key points include: retraction and intrusion of protruding maxillary incisors using segmented arch mechanics and bone screws, with a caution about irregular bony protrusions in some Asian adults; distal movement of the maxillary or mandibular dental arch using miniplates or bone screws, particularly for Class III cases with mandibular dental protrusion in Asian patients; molar protraction to close spaces using indirect anchorage; and intrusion of incisors or posterior teeth to correct deep bite or anterior open bite, emphasizing the advantages of skeletal anchorage and the challenges with periodontal involvement. The text also highlights the limitations of traditional methods and the role of modern skeletal anchorage techniques.

nodes.title: Distal Movement of Molars or the Entire Dental Arch
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses adult orthodontic treatment considerations for moving teeth and correcting bite issues using skeletal anchorage. It covers distal movement of maxillary and mandibular molars or entire arches (including Class II and Class III camouflage), molar protraction to close spaces, and intrusion of incisors and posterior teeth—particularly for open bite correction. It emphasizes the use of bone screws and miniplates, differences between adult and younger patients, and potential periodontal concerns.

nodes.title: Intrusion
key_items: Intrusion of Posterior Teeth to Close Anterior Open Bite
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers special orthodontic treatment considerations for adults, focusing on skeletal anchorage techniques for tooth movement. Main points include:

- Distal movement of maxillary molars or entire arch using miniplates or palatal bone screws; mandibular distalization now possible with skeletal anchorage for specific Class III or incisor protrusion cases.
- Molar protraction using indirect anchorage from bone screws in the palate or mandibular buccal shelf/ramus.
- Intrusion of incisors for deep bite/excessive gingival display, emphasizing skeletal anchorage and segmented archwires; caution about periodontal effects.
- Intrusion of posterior teeth to correct anterior open bite, with details on anchorage options (zygomatic miniplates, long bone screws), force systems, and transpalatal arches/splints.
- Presentation of clinical study outcomes (Scheffler et al.) on maxillary molar intrusion: mean changes, variability, relapse rates, lower molar eruption effects, and long-term stability.
- Summary of patient and orthodontist perceptions of miniplates: minimal pain, high satisfaction, ease of use.
- Concluding summary noting the growth of adult orthodontic treatment and increased collaboration with dental colleagues.

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the use of miniplates as temporary skeletal anchorage in adult orthodontic treatment, focusing on patient and clinician experiences. It reports patient-rated pain and swelling levels, noting minimal pain during surgery and active intrusion, with some postsurgical swelling. Patient satisfaction after one year was high, with most patients having better-than-expected experiences. Clinician feedback is also covered: surgeons rated the placement procedure as relatively easy with short average time, and orthodontists reported lower actual treatment difficulty compared to their anticipated difficulty, with high satisfaction and willingness to use miniplates again. The text concludes with a summary on the growth of adult orthodontic treatment, now comprising nearly 30% of patients, and the increased collaboration between orthodontists and dental colleagues.

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the use of miniplates as temporary skeletal anchors in adult orthodontic treatment, focusing on patient and clinician experiences. It reports patient-rated pain and swelling after placement (minimal pain, moderate swelling), high patient satisfaction (83% found it better than expected, 73% didn't mind the anchor), and favorable clinician feedback: surgeons rated the placement procedure as easy (mean 1.7 on a 4-point scale) with an average placement time of 15 minutes. Orthodontists initially expected treatment to be difficult but found actual treatment easy or moderately easy, and all would use miniplates again, with high satisfaction (3.8 out of 4). The text then summarizes broader trends: adult orthodontic treatment has grown from nearly zero to about 30% of patients, and orthodontists increasingly collaborate with dental colleagues to address the wider dental needs of adults.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document covers two main sections. First, it discusses the use of miniplates as temporary skeletal anchorage in adult orthodontic treatment, reporting patient and orthodontist perceptions: patients experienced minimal pain during surgery and essentially none during intrusion, though some reported significant post-surgical swelling; 83% found the experience better than expected, and 73% did not mind the miniplate. Orthodontists rated the placement procedure as easy (1.7 on a 1-4 scale), with an average placement time of 15 minutes; initially anticipated treatment difficulty decreased substantially, and all orthodontists reported high satisfaction and willingness to use miniplates again. The summary notes that adult orthodontic treatment has grown to nearly 30% of patients, and skeletal anchorage has expanded treatment possibilities, increasing orthodontists' collaboration with dental colleagues. The second part introduces a chapter on clear aligners in adults, covering aligners versus fixed treatment, benefits and limitations, and challenges. It highlights adults' preference for esthetics and lifestyle flexibility, the visibility of attachments, the need for in-person visits for key steps, comparisons of aligner and brace effectiveness (aligners may take longer for mild cases), the impact of exposed tooth structure and restorations, slower tooth movement in non-growing adults requiring adjusted aligner wear or staging, and specific adult challenges such as lack of growth, restorations, worn/missing teeth, multidisciplinary needs, and compliance.

structure.title: Clear Aligners in Adults
structure.summary: The partial document provides an outline and initial sections of a chapter on clear aligners in adults. It covers the comparison between aligners and fixed treatment in adults, the benefits and limitations of aligners, and the specific challenges encountered in adult patients. Key topics include patient esthetic concerns, treatment flexibility, the impact of adult dentition (e.g., restorations, exposed tooth structure, and aging on tooth movement), and general challenges such as compliance and multidisciplinary needs. The outline also lists comprehensive treatment topics ranging from mild to complex cases, hybrid treatments, limited treatments, handling missing teeth, and orthognathic surgery.

nodes.title: Aligners Versus Fixed Treatment in Adults
nodes.summary: The partial document introduces the topic of clear aligner treatment in adult patients. It opens with a chapter outline covering aligner versus fixed treatment, benefits/limitations, challenges, and comprehensive treatment categories (mild, moderate, complex, hybrid, limited treatment, etc.). The main content begins by discussing aligners versus fixed treatment in adults, noting adult preferences for esthetics and lifestyle flexibility, while acknowledging attachments/aligners are slightly visible and some in-person visits are required. It then details the benefits and limitations of aligners in adults, including similar overall pros/cons as in adolescents, but with adult-specific factors such as increased exposed tooth structure for retention, heavily restored dentitions favoring aligners, slower tooth movement velocity in non-growing patients, and challenges in determining the cause of poor tracking (compliance, design, or biology). Next, the document covers challenges in adult patients, emphasizing lack of growth, which makes skeletal/occlusal corrections more difficult; common issues like tooth wear, restorations, periodontal disease, and missing teeth; the need for multidisciplinary communication and 3D digital planning for restorative coordination; and compliance/burnout, including data on wear compliance and the typical waning of adherence over long treatment times. Finally, it begins discussing comprehensive treatment, noting that while ideal correction is still the goal, compromises may be necessary and informed consent is crucial. It introduces the mild difficulty category, which involves mostly intra-arch movements (crowding/spacing) with minimal root movement, and highlights the frequent use of interproximal reduction in adults to address tooth-size discrepancies, mild A-P deviations, and black triangles.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the treatment of adults with clear aligners, emphasizing key challenges and clinical considerations. It highlights the importance of 3D simulation for occlusal planning, but also addresses patient compliance and burnout with aligner wear, noting that full-time wear (20-22 hours/day) is biologically necessary and that compliance often declines after 12 months. Comprehensive treatment aims to correct occlusal discrepancies, though compromises may be needed, requiring informed consent. Cases are categorized by difficulty: mild cases involve predictable intra-arch movements and often use interproximal reduction; moderate challenges include rotations, crossbites, and A-P corrections using elastics, with careful attention to space creation and tooth tracking; complex cases require significant doctor involvement, modified staging, overcorrection, and frequent refinement aligners. Hybrid treatment combines aligners with fixed appliances, miniscrews, or splints for challenging scenarios. Root uprighting for missing-tooth spaces can be done with aligners if adequate attachment surface exists, otherwise limited braces are used. Deep bite correction in adults is more difficult due to lack of growth, relying on bite ramps, posterior attachments, and incisor proclination; severe overbite cases may need braces, but aligners can be the best option when lower tooth wear precludes braces.

nodes.title: Hybrid Treatment
nodes.summary:
This section covers the use of clear aligners in adult patients, focusing on complex case management. Key points include:

- Treating complex cases with aligners requires significant provider involvement; standard digital setups need modification, tooth movements are often reduced, adjunctive appliances (braces, TADs) are frequently needed, and progress records with revision aligners are commonly required.
- Extraction cases with aligners demand good anchorage, well-designed attachments, and careful staging for successful root control and tooth movement.
- Hybrid treatment combining aligners with fixed appliances and miniscrews is useful for challenging adult cases, such as significant or unilateral open bites.
- Root uprighting of tipped teeth adjacent to missing teeth can sometimes be done with aligners alone using large attachments, but limited braces may be needed when surface area is inadequate.
- Deep bite correction in adults is more challenging due to lack of vertical growth; aligners can achieve correction using bite ramps, posterior attachments, and incisor proclination. Severe cases may require lower braces, though aligners can be the best option when tooth wear or occlusal clearance limits brace placement.
- Limited treatment with aligners is advantageous for minor relapse or crowding because individual teeth can be moved with minimal side effects while maintaining posterior occlusion.

nodes.title: Limited Treatment
nodes.summary: This partial document covers the use of clear aligners for limited orthodontic treatment in adults. It highlights the advantage of moving individual teeth with fewer side effects, using the full dentition as anchorage. Specific clinical applications discussed include correcting minor crowding/relapse after orthodontic treatment, managing mild spacing and midline diastemas (with attention to Bolton discrepancies and overbite), and addressing minor occlusal changes such as edge-to-edge relationships from late mandibular growth or sleep appliances, sometimes using Class III elastics. The text also presents detailed case examples with figures, including deep bite correction via intrusion, and begins to address the challenge of missing teeth by describing painted aligners with virtual pontics.

nodes.title: Other Challenges
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the application of clear aligners in adult patients, focusing on limited treatment scenarios and special considerations. It covers the use of aligners for deep bite cases with abraded teeth, mild spacing including midline diastemas (with attention to Bolton discrepancies and overbite), and minor occlusal changes such as those from late mandibular growth or airway appliances. The text also addresses challenges like missing teeth, presenting solutions such as painted aligners with virtual pontics, removable pontics or wax, and cantilever bridges. Additionally, it explores the role of aligners in orthognathic surgery, detailing methods for intermaxillary fixation using bonded buttons or temporary anchorage devices (TADs) and the post-surgical management of aligner wear.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document covers the use of clear aligners in preparation for orthognathic surgery, including a figure showing surgical cases with attachments and temporary anchorage devices. It also includes references on clear aligner therapy effectiveness and compliance. The main section outlines a chapter on combined surgical and orthodontic treatment, discussing topics such as the development of orthognathic surgery, the decision between camouflage and surgery, treatment planning, contemporary surgical techniques, postsurgical stability, and the coordination of surgical and orthodontic care. It provides historical context on the evolution of orthognathic surgery from early mandibular procedures to modern techniques like sagittal split osteotomy, Le Fort I downfracture, rigid fixation, and distraction osteogenesis.

structure.title: Combined Surgical and Orthodontic Treatment
structure.summary:
The partial document introduces combined surgical and orthodontic treatment for severe orthodontic problems that cannot be addressed by growth modification or camouflage. It highlights the necessity of coordinating surgery with orthodontics and other dental treatment. The main points covered include:

- The chapter outline, listing key topics such as development of orthognathic surgery, the borderline patient (camouflage versus surgery), malocclusion severity, extraction decisions, temporary skeletal anchorage, esthetic and psychosocial considerations, treatment planning with simulation, contemporary surgical techniques (mandibular, maxillary, dentoalveolar, distraction osteogenesis, adjunctive facial procedures, OSA-related surgery, soft tissue surgery), postsurgical stability, special planning considerations (timing, combined vertical and anteroposterior problems), and the integration of surgical and orthodontic treatment (appliance considerations, presurgical orthodontics, patient management at operation, postoperative care, postsurgical orthodontics).

- The beginning of the "Development of Orthognathic Surgery" section, tracing its history from early 20th-century body ostectomy, through the introduction of the sagittal split ramus osteotomy in 1957, to maxillary surgery advances culminating in the Le Fort I downfracture technique. It notes progress in the 1980s (repositioning jaws, chin, dentoalveolar segments), 1990s (rigid internal fixation, improved stability), and the advent of distraction osteogenesis for severe cases.

nodes.title: Development of Orthognathic Surgery
nodes.summary: This partial document introduces combined surgical and orthodontic treatment for severe dentofacial problems. It outlines the development and historical evolution of orthognathic surgery, including key techniques such as sagittal split ramus osteotomy, Le Fort I downfracture surgery, rigid internal fixation, and distraction osteogenesis. It discusses indications for surgery versus camouflage treatment, the envelope of discrepancy and limits of orthodontic tooth movement, and factors in deciding between surgery and temporary skeletal anchorage. The document also emphasizes the importance of esthetic and psychosocial considerations, treatment planning with simulation of alternative outcomes using digital technologies, and contemporary surgical techniques for the mandible, maxilla, and dentoalveolar structures. It highlights presurgical orthodontics, surgical coordination, postoperative care, and postsurgical orthodontic treatment, supported by a clinical case example and imaging/3D-printed planning tools.

nodes.title: The Borderline Patient: Camouflage Versus Surgery
nodes.summary: The partial document covers combined surgical and orthodontic treatment for severe dentofacial problems, emphasizing the use of digital technologies, cone beam imaging, and 3D planning tools. It discusses the borderline patient and the decision between orthodontic camouflage and surgery, including the envelope of discrepancy, extraction planning differences, and factors affecting camouflage success. It compares orthognathic surgery with temporary skeletal anchorage, addresses esthetic and psychosocial considerations, and highlights the importance of patient expectations and psychological adjustment. The document also describes treatment planning with simulation of alternative outcomes, the evolution from 2D cephalometric tracing to 3D virtual surgical planning, and a hybrid approach combining both methods. Contemporary surgical techniques and the types of jaw movements possible with orthognathic surgery are also outlined.

nodes.title: Contemporary Surgical Techniques
nodes.summary: The partial document covers combined surgical and orthodontic treatment in adults, beginning with a detailed case example of computer-assisted orthognathic surgery planning using 2D and 3D software, including simultaneous rhinoplasty, mandibular advancement, and chin osteotomy. It then outlines contemporary surgical techniques for jaw repositioning, covering mandibular surgery (sagittal split osteotomy, lower border osteotomy) and maxillary surgery (Le Fort I osteotomy, segmental osteotomy, surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion). The text also addresses dentoalveolar surgery, including management of inadvertent tooth movement and repositioning of alveolar segments, as well as distraction osteogenesis and its indications. Adjunctive facial procedures are discussed, such as chin augmentation/reduction, rhinoplasty, facial implants, lip procedures, and submental procedures. The document further examines surgical procedures related to obstructive sleep apnea, including maxillomandibular advancement, soft tissue surgeries, and hypoglossal nerve stimulation. Finally, it reviews postsurgical stability, presenting a hierarchy of stability for different jaw movements and factors influencing stability, and ends with special considerations in surgical planning, particularly the timing of surgery for progressive deformities like asymmetric mandibular deficiency.

nodes.title: Special Considerations in Planning Surgical Treatment
nodes.summary: The partial document covers special considerations in planning combined surgical and orthodontic treatment for adults, focusing on the timing of orthognathic surgery in relation to growth. It discusses progressive deformities such as asymmetric mandibular deficiency and excess, including hemimandibular hyperplasia, its characteristics, and when early surgery is indicated. It addresses symmetric excess growth, growth deficiency, and the rationale for delaying mandibular or maxillary advancement until growth is completed, while acknowledging psychosocial exceptions. The document also covers correction of combined vertical and anteroposterior problems: increasing anterior face height in short-face Class II patients is best achieved through mandibular ramus surgery, whereas decreasing face height in long-face patients is best achieved through maxillary (Le Fort I) osteotomy. Additional special planning points include management of incision lines and gingival tissue, removal of third molars before ramus surgery, discussion of temporomandibular dysfunction, and speech distortion considerations. Finally, it outlines the integration of surgical and orthodontic treatment: orthodontic appliance selection (fixed edgewise, self-ligating, ceramic, lingual, or clear aligners), goals and steps of presurgical orthodontics, and the approach to leveling the mandibular arch (e.g., deferring extrusion of posterior teeth until after surgery).

nodes.title: Putting Surgical and Orthodontic Treatment Together: Who Does What and When?
nodes.summary: The partial document covers key aspects of combined surgical and orthodontic treatment, beginning with speech distortions in Class II, III, and open bite patients and the variable impact of orthognathic surgery on speech. It then discusses orthodontic appliance considerations for surgery, including fixed appliances, ceramic bracket limitations, lingual appliances, and clear aligners. The presurgical orthodontic phase is detailed, covering goals such as preparing teeth without concern for occlusion, steps for arch alignment, leveling of mandibular and maxillary arches, establishing incisor position and space closure, the surgery-first approach, and stabilizing archwires. The document also addresses patient management at the operation, including final surgical planning, the use of splints and stabilization, and postoperative care. Finally, it describes postsurgical orthodontics, including archwire selection, elastic use, and retention considerations, with illustrative case examples demonstrating clear tray treatment, customized appliances with virtual surgical planning, and segmental maxillary osteotomy combined with rhinoplasty and genioplasty.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The partial document contains a continuation of a figure legend (U and V) describing posttreatment cephalometric imaging and superimposition, highlighting the role of genioplasty in chin positioning and rhinoplasty in nasal tip control for facial balance. It is followed by an extensive reference list (numbered 1–45) covering orthognathic surgery topics, including surgical techniques, treatment stability, soft tissue prediction, psychosocial outcomes, obstructive sleep apnea, speech effects, and surgery-first approaches.

structure.title: Index
structure.summary: This partial document is the index of a comprehensive orthodontic textbook. It covers a wide range of topics, including: basic orthodontic concepts, classifications of malocclusion, craniofacial growth and development from infancy through adolescence, and the biological basis of tooth movement and orthodontic therapy. It details various treatment approaches such as fixed and removable appliances, functional appliances, clear aligner therapy, orthognathic (surgical) correction, and adjunctive procedures. It also addresses specific clinical problems like Class II and Class III malocclusions, crowding, open bites, deep bites, crossbites, impacted teeth, and space management in both preadolescent and adult patients. Further entries cover diagnostic tools and records (cephalometric analysis, imaging, study models), treatment planning, retention and relapse, an extensive glossary of mechanics and forces, and considerations for patient management and temporomandibular disorders. The index reflects the scope of a full orthodontic curriculum, touching on both clinical procedures and the scientific principles that underpin them.
